activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: In 1966, Pope Paul VI's Paenitemini allowed national bishops' conferences to replace the traditional Catholic fast and abstinence with other penance, such as prayer and works of charity.
story:
Alexandra found her grandmother in the kitchen on a Friday afternoon, slicing eggplants into coins, and asked the question she had been carrying since the debate club announced its next topic. "Grandma, why do we still skip meat on Fridays when the Hendersons don't? They go to Saint Brigid's same as us."

The knife paused above the cutting board. "Because that's what we do," her grandmother said, which Alexandra had learned, over seventeen years of Fridays, meant the conversation was supposed to be over. But the debate assignment was due Monday, and the motion was whether an ancient religious rule still applied in modern life, and Mr. Kobayashi had insisted they argue from the text itself, not from habit or feeling.

"It's not just because we do," Alexandra said. "There has to be a reason, or there used to be one. Can I look in your study?"

Her grandmother waved the knife toward the hall, already stirring oil in the pan, and Alexandra went to the bookshelf where the old leather volumes stood in their soft order. She was looking for the documents of the Second Vatican Council, because she remembered her father saying once, vaguely, that everything about Friday meat had changed in the sixties. What she found instead was a pamphlet, thin and foxed at the edges, tucked between a missal and a book on Marian apparitions. On the cover, a word she didn't know: Paenitemini.

She sat cross-legged on the rug and read. It was a letter from 1966, from Pope Paul VI. It said that the traditional Catholic fast and abstinence, the whole Friday discipline her grandmother still kept, could be replaced by other penance, and that the choice belonged to the national bishops' conferences. Prayer, or works of charity, could stand in for the skipped meat. Alexandra read the paragraph twice, feeling something shift in her chest, the strange invigoration of discovering that a rule she had thought was stone was actually a door.

She carried the pamphlet back to the kitchen and set it on the counter beside the eggplant. "Grandma, look. In 1966, Pope Paul VI wrote this, and it let the bishops' conferences here decide to replace the Friday fast and abstinence with other penance instead. Prayer, or charity work. So you don't have to do this."

Her grandmother dried her hands slowly on the towel. She picked up the pamphlet and turned it over, and Alexandra watched her face for the sign of defeat, the moment the old woman would concede to a document she had perhaps never read. It didn't come. Instead her grandmother smoothed the page like something living.

"I know that letter," she said. "Sister Ruth read parts of it to us my last year of school. We thought it was wonderful, all that freedom." She set the pamphlet down and took up the knife again, laying another coin of eggplant in the hot oil, where it hissed. "Your great-grandmother kept the meatless Fridays anyway. She said the point was the giving up, not the rule. That if she could choose her penance, she would choose something too easy, because she knew herself." A pause, the spitting of oil, the window going amber. "Maybe she was right and maybe she wasn't. I've never decided."

From where the grandmother stood, the girl looked suddenly younger than seventeen, sitting on the kitchen stool with the pamphlet in her lap, frowning at it the way she used to frown at multiplication tables. The grandmother could see the debate assembling itself behind the girl's eyes, the two sides being sorted like cards, and she felt a tenderness for that effort, and also a small ache, because the girl would want an answer and there wasn't one.

"So which side do I argue?" Alexandra said. "The rule changed, but you didn't. Is that fidelity or stubbornness?"

"Argue what the text says," her grandmother said, "and then tell them what your great-grandmother said, and tell them you don't know which is better. Honest people lose debates and win something else."

Alexandra laughed, and the sound came out ebullient, louder than the kitchen was used to. She texted Mylee a photo of the pamphlet's cover, and Mylee wrote back within a minute, asking what Paenitemini meant, and Alexandra, curious now about the etymology, found the Latin root at the bottom of a footnote: to repent, to make oneself do without. She read it aloud, and her grandmother nodded as though she had known it all along.

They ate the eggplant with bread and sharp cheese while the light failed over the back fence, and Alexandra pushed the pamphlet to the center of the table where they could both see it, its cover turned toward her grandmother's empty plate.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Hokusai's print series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, made around 1830 to 1832, actually contains 46 prints, because ten were added after the first 36 sold well.
story:
Mr. Pierre kept the portfolio room open on Thursdays, and by late October Brooke had claimed the table nearest the window, where the afternoon light fell across her sketchbook at an angle she liked. The assignment was simple to say and impossible to do: ten artworks, one theme, an artist's statement to hold them together. She had eleven. She had, if she was honest, fourteen, and the fourteenth was the one she could not stop thinking about.

The theme had come to her in September, standing on the overpass above the rail line with Bethany, watching freight cars slide beneath their feet. Gates, she had written that night. Not fences, not walls, gates. The ones that open and the ones that are only painted shut. Since then she had drawn the school's chained side door, her grandmother's garden gate in February, the ticket barrier at the station, a rusted farm gate she'd photographed from the car on the way to Penelope's cousin's wedding. The drawings were good. That was the problem. She could not tell which one to cut.

"You're over the limit," Penelope said, leaning over the table on Thursday, chewing the end of a pencil she had borrowed from Brooke three weeks ago. "Eleven is over the limit."

"I know it's over the limit."

"Mr. Pierre counts. He counted Dev's."

"I know he counts." Brooke pulled the newest piece toward her, the one she had started at midnight: a turnstile at the community pool, half in shadow, the ticket window behind it lit like an altar. The perspective had taken her two hours. It enthralled her in a way she distrusted, the way certain pieces seduce you into keeping them past their usefulness. She slid it into the folder anyway.

Bethany arrived with a library book wedged under her arm, a heavy thing with a wave on the cover, blue and cream, a tiny boat riding the curl. She dropped it on the table between them. "I was looking at composition stuff for my statement and I found this guy. Hokusai. Japanese, prints. He did this whole series about Mount Fuji, and guess what, it's called Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji."

"So it's thirty-six prints," Penelope said.

"That's the thing. It's forty-six." Bethany flipped to the back of the book, where the later prints were reproduced smaller, four to a page. "It's actually forty-six prints, because ten were added after the first thirty-six sold well. Around 1830 to 1832, the whole thing. People wanted more, so he made more, and the title stayed wrong."

Brooke looked at the book. She looked for a long time. There was a print of a wave, and there was one of thunderstorms below the summit, and there was one where the mountain appeared through a round window, framed by someone's everyday kitchen. Forty-six views. The title had promised thirty-six and the world had answered with ten more, and nobody, apparently, had minded.

"That doesn't help me," she said. "I still have to hand in ten."

"Obviously," Bethany said. "But it's not about you."

That evening Brooke spread all fourteen pieces across her bedroom floor, embryonic ones and finished ones, and sat among them with a mug of tea going cold. She had been thinking of the portfolio as a container, a gate that closed after ten. But the Hokusai thing kept circling back. He had made thirty-six, and they had sold, and then he had made ten more, and the series was not ruined by that, it was enlarged. The theme was not the number. The theme was the mountain, always the mountain, seen from wherever he happened to be standing.

She began to sort differently. Not which pieces were best, but which pieces saw the gate from the same place. The turnstile and the ticket barrier were the same drawing twice, honestly. The garden gate and the chained door were the same drawing too, warm and cold versions of it. She let the turnstile go, and the barrier, and was surprised at how little it hurt. What remained were ten views, each one a slightly different angle on the same locked and opening thing, and the fourteenth piece, the midnight one, could wait. It was not being cut. It was being added, later, after the first ten had done their work, if anyone wanted more.

The artist's statement took her forty minutes. She wrote about gates as decisions, about how a gate is only a gate from one side and a wall from the other, and she ended it with a sentence she underlined once and then did not underline again.

On Friday she carried the folder to Mr. Pierre's desk. He counted the pieces the way Bethany said he would, touching each corner with one finger, and when he reached ten he looked up. "And the eleventh?" he asked, because of course he had seen her working on it, because he counted everything.

Brooke smiled and zipped the folder shut. "Ask me again when it sells."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: On level ground without air resistance, the time of flight equals twice the initial vertical velocity divided by g, because rising and falling take equal times.
story:
Lauren had planned to spend the Saturday before finals at her desk, but her desk had become a place where highlighters went to die, so she carried her physics notebook out to the backyard instead, along with a soccer ball, a garden hose, and the stopwatch function on her phone, which she had never once used for anything legitimate.

Wyatt was already lying in the grass by the fence, sunglasses on, a bag of chips balanced on his chest like a small, salty pet. "You're studying outside," he said. "Voluntarily."

"I'm conducting science," Lauren said. She dropped the ball on his stomach. The chips survived. "I have a physics test Monday and I don't understand a single problem in chapter four. Every one of them involves something being launched."

"Like a missile."

"Like a soccer ball. Like a, what was the one, a stunt motorcyclist driving off a cliff." She sat down cross-legged and opened the notebook. Dahlia arrived ten minutes later through the side gate, holding her own textbook, because Dahlia was the sort of person who heard "study session" and brought reinforcements.

The problem Lauren had circled twice was simple enough on its face: a ball leaves the ground at some angle, and you have to find how long it stays in the air. The book wanted her to split the launch into two pieces, a sideways piece and an up-and-down piece, and treat them as though they had never met. That was the part she resented. The ball did not know it had components. The ball was a single object doing a single arcing thing, and yet the math insisted on cutting it in half, an aisle down the middle of the ball's soul.

She worked one anyway, following the example in the book like a trail of breadcrumbs. She found how long the ball took to reach the top of its arc, wrote that number in the answer blank, and felt a small, satisfying click of completion.

"That's it?" Dahlia said, reading over her shoulder. "You found when it gets to the top."

"And then it's done."

"And then it comes down," Dahlia said. "The ball does come down. I've seen it happen."

Lauren looked at the number. Then she looked at the soccer ball. Then she looked at the answer in the back of the book, which was exactly twice her number, sitting there like a smug little verdict. "Okay," she said. "Field research."

The experiment, such as it was, went like this. Lauren stood at the far end of the yard and threw the ball straight up, trying to keep it from drifting sideways, while Dahlia timed the flight and Wyatt called out the height of the peak with the confidence of a man who had no way to measure it. "Nine meters," he said. "Ten. Twelve. Call it twelve." Dahlia ignored him. Ms. Campbell, watering her tomatoes on the other side of the hedge, watched over the fence with the expression of a neighbor deciding whether this was a thing to call someone's mother about, and then, judiciously, went back to her tomatoes.

Lauren threw it up softly, so it hung for about a second and a half total. Then she threw it harder, and Dahlia's stopwatch read three seconds and change. Lauren had her write both numbers in the notebook, side by side.

"Watch it," Lauren said, and threw again. "The way up and the way down look the same."

"They take the same time," Dahlia said, squinting at the stopwatch. "The whole flight is just the way up twice."

Lauren sat down in the grass and did the arithmetic. The book's rule for the time to the top was the initial up-and-down speed divided by g, that little 9.8 that showed up in every problem like an unwanted relative. So the whole flight, up and then down, was twice that: twice the initial vertical velocity divided by g. Which was exactly the back-of-the-book answer, which was exactly twice her answer, which meant her problem wasn't physics at all. Her problem was that she had stopped at the top of the arc and closed the book on a ball still hanging in the air.

"So the total time is just double the time up," she said, mostly to the notebook.

"Groundbreaking," said Wyatt, without lifting his sunglasses.

"It is, actually, for me." She reworked three problems, doubling each time, and the answers came out clean, one after another, like a row of freshly ironed shirts. The splitting stopped feeling like a betrayal of the ball and started feeling like a trick she was allowed to play on it. She could handle the sideways part and the vertical part separately, in two little columns, and then let the ball be whole again at the end. It was less like dissecting something and more like taking it apart to move it through a doorway.

The only thing she still couldn't account for was air, which the book cheerfully told her to ignore, and which the actual backyard kept supplying. Her throws drifted. The measured times came out a hair long or a hair short, never quite landing on the arithmetic, and she wrote in the margin, "real air, real ball, approximately," and underlined approximately twice. She did not know yet what to do about that gap, or whether later chapters would hand her the tools, and she decided she could dislike that on Monday.

"Vote," Wyatt said eventually, sitting up and letting the chip bag fall. "Continue studying out here, or go inside where the chips and the wifi are. All in favor of inside."

"That's not a plebiscite," Dahlia said, "that's just you wanting to leave."

"I'm not disenfranchising anyone. Lauren gets a vote. The tomatoes get a vote."

"The tomatoes have been very quiet on the issue," Lauren said. She closed the notebook, put her thumb on the stopwatch, and threw the ball up one more time, high, the way that made the whole yard go still while it hung there at the top of its arc. "Half," she said, watching it pause. The ball came down. Dahlia clicked the watch.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections.
story:
The waiting room of the Belsize Clinic had exactly fourteen chairs and Isla had counted them twice, once at 3:40 and once at 3:52, because the clock above the reception desk was mercurial in a way clocks should not be, seeming to jump forward whenever she looked away. She was there for a training session. Ms. Becker, who taught health and coached field hockey and seemed to have opinions about everything except her own volume control, had arranged it: three seniors, trained by the clinic as peer educators, would run the information table at the school's autumn fair. Isla had volunteered mostly because Esme had, and now Esme was late, which was itself a form of consistency.

"You're the student volunteer," said the nurse at the desk, checking a list. "Isla? Go on back to the small room. We're doing contraception first, consent second, testing last, and if you mix them up nobody dies, but people do get confused."

The small room had a flip chart with three pages already written. Kaila was there, spinning a marker between her fingers like a tiny, unsuccessful baton. "Esme's coming," she said, before Isla could ask. "She texted. Something about a bus and a pigeon. The pigeon was the problem, not the bus."

The training was faster than Isla expected. The nurse, whose badge said TRAINER rather than a name, laid out the methods one by one, the pill, the implant, the ring, IUDs, condoms, and had each of them repeat back the basics until Kaila stopped saying "the thing with the hormones" and started saying actual words. Then they practised the consent piece, which was harder to put on a flip chart. "You explain it like a gate," the nurse said. "It can be opened at any time and closed at any time, and it has to be opened by the person who owns it, every single time, no matter what it said last week." Isla wrote that down and underlined it, then underlined it again, because at the fair she would have to say it out loud to people she had known since Reception, some of whom had seen her cry over a lost mitten.

It was the testing station that snagged her. When the nurse explained how someone could come to the clinic, with or without an appointment, and get tested for infections, Kaila asked the question Isla had been circling without landing on. "So if someone's on the pill," Kaila said, "they're covered for that too, right?"

"No," the nurse said, and Isla felt the whole afternoon recalibrate around that single word. "Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections." She said it plainly, no drama, and moved on to the mouth swab demonstration, and Isla sat there thinking about how many times she had half-assumed otherwise without ever actually thinking it.

On the way home, the three of them stopped at the pharmacy by the bus stop, because Esme had declared that if they were going to be peer educators they should know what the actual shelves looked like. It was Esme, finally arrived, pigeon incident apparently resolved, who did the bold thing. She carried her little sister's eczema cream to the counter and then, with the smoothness of someone who had rehearsed in the deodorant aisle, asked the pharmacist, "Quick question, if someone has a prescription for birth control, does that protect against infections too?"

The pharmacist, a man with reading glasses pushed up into grey hair, said, "No, it doesn't. Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of those." He looked at the three of them, standing there in their matching school scarves, and something in his face softened. "Peer educators?"

"Terrifyingly," said Kaila.

"You'll do fine," he said. "Most people your age think you can't get tested without a parent. Tell them anyone can walk into that clinic."

That was the thing Isla hadn't known she'd wanted until she had it. On the bus home she flipped open her notebook and drafted the fair table plan in the margin of her history notes, which was a mistake, because the history notes were on Gregor Mendel and her draft now read: STEP ONE, GATE METAPHOR, STEP TWO, phenotype ratio 9:3:3:1. Kaila leaned over and read it. "Bold curriculum," she said. "You're going to explain consent through pea plants."

"It's the only part of my education that's sticking," Isla said. "Everything else is a suggestion."

Esme, across the aisle, was quieter than usual, and when they got off at their stop she said, walking backwards ahead of them so she could face them, "You know I only signed up because you two did. But that gate thing. I liked the gate thing." She turned around before Isla could decide whether that was a confession or a joke, and started walking fast, and Isla and Kaila had to trot to catch up, both of them calling her name down the street toward the fish and chip shop, whose lit sign had, as always, exactly one letter gone dark, so that it read F SH AND CH PS, and Esme, laughing now, pointed at it and said, "That's what I'll put on our poster."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: Most of Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights, published in 1847, is told by the housekeeper Nelly Dean to the visitor Lockwood, so events reach readers through two narrators with their own biases.
story:
Nicolas had told Corbin he would be at the library by four, and it was already ten past, and the lie had come out of him so smoothly that he had almost believed it himself. He set his backpack on the corner table by the window, the one with the wobbly leg he liked to brace with his heel, and took out the novel. Wuthering Heights, the cover soft with age, borrowed from his mother's shelf. He had a paper due in September, his first for the college course he was technically still too nervous to call a college course, and the prompt asked one question: can you trust the person telling you this story?

Corbin dropped into the opposite chair without a greeting, the way he did everything, as if arrival were a settled matter. "You said four."

"I said four-ish," Nicolas said, which was not what he had said, and he noticed that he had noticed, and filed the noticing away the way Ms. Yip had taught him to flag things in the margins. She was shelving returns two aisles over; he could hear the wheels of her cart squeaking in their patient, irregular rhythm.

He opened the book to his sticky notes. The whole thing, he had discovered at midnight, was a story inside a story. Most of it was told by the housekeeper, Nelly Dean, to a visitor named Lockwood, and Lockwood wrote it all down. So nothing reached him straight. Every event passed through two people first, and each of them had reasons of their own. He read a passage aloud, half to Corbin and half to the window. "She calls Heathcliff a fiend. Says it like it's a fact. Like she's just reporting the weather."

"Isn't she, though?" Corbin had flipped the book toward himself and was squinting at the florid prose with open distrust, as if the long clauses were personally inconveniencing him. "He sounds awful."

"That's the thing." Nicolas turned the book back around. "We only know he's awful because of her. Watch what she does when Catherine gets sick. Nelly's right there, and she half admits she goaded her, and then she keeps the whole thing from Edgar, and then she tells us about it years later like she was a helpless witness. Is that a fiend report or a self-defense?"

Corbin leaned back until the chair creaked. "So the paper is, like, the book is lying?"

Nicolas started to say yes and stopped, because that wasn't quite it either, and the difference interested him. Nelly wasn't lying the way a liar lies, inventing things from nothing. She was remembering, selecting, arranging. She disliked some of these people, and maybe her dislike coloured how she told their story, and there was no clean way to peel her account off the events underneath, because the account was all there was. Even Lockwood, this fussy visitor with his vanity and his affectation of worldliness, kept interrupting with his own little judgments. Two sets of hands on every scene. He wrote in the margin: the story is the telling.

Ms. Yip's cart arrived at the end of their aisle and stopped. She looked at the stack of notes, the bristling book, the two of them arguing over a hundred and seventy years old novel. "That one took me three tries," she said. "The second narrator is worse than the first, in my opinion."

"Lockwood," Nicolas said. "You think he's making things up?"

"I think he misses almost everything he sees." She squared a shelf of biographies with two fingers and moved on, and Nicolas recalibrated something in his head, quietly, without announcing it: the question wasn't whether the book lied but how much of himself each narrator had to hide.

Archer showed up at five with a granola bar and no intention of reading anything. He listened to Nicolas's theory for ninety seconds, chewing, and then said the thing that broke it open. "So if Nelly hated Heathcliff, and she's the only camera in the room, then we've never actually seen Heathcliff. Not once."

"That's the paper," Nicolas said, though it wasn't, yet. He pulled a fresh sheet toward him and wrote two columns: what Nelly saw, and what Nelly wanted. Under the second column, after a minute, he wrote a question he couldn't fill in. What did Lockwood want? He stared at it. Outside, the streetlights came on down the block in a slow, sequential wave.

"Half of this is you guessing," Corbin said, reading over his arm.

"I know. I can't tell how much is guess and how much is evidence, and I don't think the book wants me to be able to." Nicolas underlined the question twice. "So the honest paper says that."

"Honest papers don't get A's."

Ms. Yip passed again on her way to the desk, and Nicolas, almost without deciding to, asked her whether she'd ever finished it, third try. She considered the window a moment, the lights coming on outside it, and said, "I finished it. Whether I believed it is a different question." Then she pushed her cart around the corner, wheels squeaking, and Nicolas wrote at the top of the page: due September, and under it, believe what?

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In England, the Tenant Fees Act 2019 caps most tenancy deposits at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under £50,000.
story:
The open house was on Hollis Road, a narrow terrace with a hand-lettered sign taped to the letterbox. Clara had come because Mohammad swore the flats above the shops were cheap, and because Dorothy, who turned eighteen last month and had been fighting with her mother since March, needed somewhere to live by September. Mr. De Vries met them at the door with a clipboard and a set of keys that jingled like change in a pocket.

"Six hundred a month," he said, leading them up a staircase that smelled of detergent and old carpet. "One bedroom, furnished, bills not included." He said it the way a pundit on the evening news recited house prices, as though the figure were a law of nature rather than a number he had chosen. Dorothy walked the length of the sitting room twice, touching the radiator, the window latch, the peeling corner of wallpaper above the sink.

Clara asked about the deposit. Her parents had spent the spring arguing about their own mortgage, the fixed term ending, the new rate, and she had absorbed more of it than she meant to, the way she absorbed Dorothy's fights through her bedroom wall when Dorothy called at midnight. She knew that a deposit was not rent. She knew, from her mother's muttering, that when you bought instead of rented you needed a down payment, a lump sum the bank insisted on before it would lend you the rest, and that her parents had saved for theirs for six years. Renting, she had assumed, was simpler.

"Two months up front," Mr. De Vries said. "Twelve hundred, plus the first month's rent before you move in. That's standard."

Dorothy's face went carefully blank. Clara recognized the blankness; it was the one Dorothy wore when a teacher assigned something she already knew she couldn't finish. Eighteen hundred pounds before she slept a single night in the room. Dorothy worked Saturdays at the garden centre and had four hundred saved.

"It's a nice flat," Mohammad offered from the doorway, in the tone of someone trying to keep the afternoon pleasant. He was blasé about the whole enterprise because his parents owned outright and he had never once thought about what a roof cost. Clara sometimes envied him that, the way she envied people who had never had the flu.

She took out her phone and stepped onto the landing. She typed "deposit two months legal uk" and scrolled past the forums, the panicked questions from people in Dorothy's position, until she found the actual legislation with the dull certainty of an official document. The Tenant Fees Act 2019. She read the line twice. Most tenancy deposits were capped at five weeks' rent, when the annual rent was under £50,000. Six hundred a month was seven thousand two hundred a year, well under the threshold, so five weeks was the ceiling: not two months, not eight weeks, but five. Six hundred divided by four, times five. Seven hundred and fifty. She came back into the room feeling the specific steadiness of someone holding a printed fact in a hand previously empty.

"It's five weeks," she said. "Under the Tenant Fees Act 2019, when the annual rent is under fifty thousand, the deposit cap is five weeks' rent. Ours is seven hundred and fifty, not twelve hundred."

Mr. De Vries looked at her over the clipboard. "Five weeks," he repeated, as if tasting it. He was quiet long enough that Clara could hear the fridge humming in the kitchenette. She watched him recalculate something behind his eyes, some arithmetic of which tenants argue and which tenants simply pay, and she understood that the two months had not been a mistake. It had been a test of whether anyone would count.

"Most people don't check," he said finally, and began filling in a form. "Five weeks, then. Plus first month's. Thirteen fifty total." Dorothy sat down on the arm of the chair, the blankness gone, replaced by the rapid visible arithmetic of what remained in her account and how many Saturdays stood between now and September. Mohammad asked about the water pressure and Mr. De Vries turned the tap.

Clara looked at the window, at the row of chimney pots against a grey sky, and thought about her parents and their down payment, about the way owning and renting were supposed to be opposite shores with nothing between them, and about how Dorothy would hand over seven hundred and fifty pounds and never see it work for her the way a down payment works, only wait for it back at the end. She did not know yet whether that was a reason to keep renting or a reason to want the other thing, and she suspected she wouldn't know for years.

"Can I measure the bedroom?" Dorothy asked, already pulling the tape measure from her bag.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note one octave higher than another vibrates at exactly twice its frequency, so the A above A440 is 880 hertz.
story:
Eric had been coming to Ms. Novák's studio on Riparian Lane since September, and in all that time he had never once practiced the way she asked him to. The studio sat at the end of a gravel drive beside the river, and in the early lessons he had spent most of his attention watching the water slide past the window, gray-green and indifferent, while his fingers fumbled through scales. Today, though, he had brought something new: a clip-on tuner he'd bought with lunch money from the pawnshop near school.

"It's cheating," said Lilia, who took the slot before his and never left right away. She was tuning her violin by ear, as Ms. Novák insisted everyone eventually learn to do. "The whole point is to hear it."

"The whole point is to sound less terrible," Eric said. He clipped the little device to the head of his violin and drew the bow across the A string. The tuner's needle swung and settled, and the screen glowed green over the number 440.

"That's A," Lilia said, as if he didn't know, because she enjoyed knowing things he knew. "A four forty. It's like the official A. Every orchestra tunes to it. It's the zeitgeist of tuning, basically."

"That is not what that word means," Eric said, and she shrugged, unrepentant, plucking her D string and leaning toward it like someone listening for a knock at a door.

Ms. Novák came out from the back room with two glasses of water and the expression of a woman who had heard every argument her students could invent. "The tuner stays," she said, "as long as Eric tells me what it says, not just whether it's green."

So he told her. He played his A and read the number aloud, four forty, and she had him play it again, softer, and then with a wild, sawing pressure that made Lilia wince theatrically. Then she did something he hadn't expected. She reached over and placed his first finger on the E string, low and close to the nut.

"Now play that."

The note came out thin and pinched at first, and then, when he straightened his wrist the way she'd been telling him for months, it rang out clean. He glanced at the tuner and stopped bowing entirely.

"It says eight eighty."

"Play the open A again," Ms. Novák said. He did. Four forty. He played the higher one. Eight eighty. He played them in alternation, back and forth, watching the numbers flicker, and began to laugh. "One's exactly double the other. The A above A four forty is eight eighty. It's not close to double, it's exactly double." He said it again to the room, to the window, to the river that did not care. "Every octave is just, what, twice the vibrations?"

"That," said Ms. Novák, "is something you have now discovered twice, once with your eyes and once, three years ago, with your ears, if you'd been listening."

"I compartmentalize," Eric said. "Math happens at school. Music happens here. Apparently they've been the same thing the whole time and nobody filed the paperwork."

Lilia had taken the tuner from him and clipped it onto her own violin, uninvited, which he felt was rich given her position on cheating. She played her A, then slid up to the octave, watching the number double exactly, her face doing something complicated, part delight and part grievance. "Okay," she admitted. "That's actually beautiful. Why did nobody just show me that on day one instead of making me guess for two years?"

"Because," Ms. Novák said, gathering the glasses, "if I explain everything, you get answers. If you find one thing yourself, you get curious."

Eric was still stuck on the doubling. It bothered him in a pleasant way, the way a good puzzle bothers you, that the note sounded higher but the relationship between the numbers was so clean, so exact, and he did not understand what that meant about why octaves sound like the same letter. He said as much, and Ms. Novák did not explain it, which he suspected was on purpose.

He walked out with Lilia along the riparian path behind the studio, the river moving alongside them, the tuner zipped in his case. He was already planning to test every octave he could find, up and down every string, at home, tonight.

"You realize," Lilia said, kicking a pebble into the water, "that after all that, you practiced scales for forty minutes without once being asked to."

Eric looked at his watch, then at his case, then back at her.

"Don't tell Ms. Novák," he said.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: An off-book rehearsal is one where actors must perform without their scripts, having memorised their lines.
story:
The rehearsal space was a converted gym at the far end of the drama camp, its floor taped with bright blue rectangles where the set would be. Laurie stood on a folding chair at the edge of it, her blocking notes curled in one hand, watching Crystal hold her script like a shield. Tomorrow night was the showing for the whole camp, and tomorrow morning, Laurie had announced on Sunday, they would go off-book. "Off-book means no scripts in your hands," she had said then, trying to sound like someone who had directed before. "Memorised. All of it." Crystal had nodded, and Laurie had believed her.

"Take it again from the doorway," Laurie called. "Khloe, you cross downstage left, and Crystal, you follow two counts behind her. Like we blocked it Tuesday." Khloe moved, quick and sure, but Crystal stayed planted near the door, script open, her eyes flicking down every third word. The silence between their lines stretched until it snapped.

"Crystal. You're carrying the binder."

"I know." Crystal turned a page that didn't need turning. "I'm off-book for like most of it."

Laurie climbed down from the chair. The camp's director, Mr. Delgado, had told them that a student director's job was to serve the play, not her own ego, and she had written that in her notebook like scripture. But she was learning that the sentence hid a choice inside it. She could protect Crystal's feelings and let the scene go soft, or she could push, and risk making Crystal decide that theatre was a place where people impugned your effort for fun. There was a version of directing that was all generosity, and a version that was all pressure, and Laurie had watched both fail in other groups that week. She didn't want to be either of those directors. What she wanted, she was beginning to understand, was to be the one who could tell the difference between an actor who was lazy and an actor who was afraid, and she did not yet fully trust herself to know which she was looking at.

"Can I see the script a second?" she asked. Crystal handed it over, and Laurie flipped through the pages, careful not to read like a judge. There were pencil marks everywhere, tiny arrows, half the lines underlined twice. This was not a lazy person's script. This was a frightened person's script, or maybe a capricious memory's, lines memorised on Monday and gone by Wednesday, rewritten each night by a brain that refused to hold still. Laurie had read that some actors memorised best on their feet, in the body, and some memorised by rote at a desk, and she had no idea which kind Crystal was, and no time to find out gently.

"Here's what we'll do," Laurie said. "We don't wait for tomorrow morning. We do it right now, tonight, just you and me and Khloe if she'll stay. But we do it differently. Khloe, sit down." Khloe folded onto the floor, curious, and Laurie closed the binder and set it on the far side of the tape, in the dead zone where no blocking ever went. "Crystal, you stand in the doorway. Don't come in. Just your first line."

"I'll forget the second."

"Then you stand in silence until you find it, and I'll hold up the binder if you're truly stuck. The scene can hold silence. It can't hold the pages." It sounded harsher than she meant it, and she softened without taking it back. "Nobody's judging. Khloe's on her phone. I'm the only one listening, and I'm on your side."

They ran it. Crystal dried twice, once for a long time, her face going red in the fluorescent light, and Laurie held the binder up without a word and let Crystal snatch a single line from it before it came down again. On the fourth pass something shifted; the following cross worked, Crystal two counts behind Khloe exactly, her hands empty and doing something with themselves that wasn't holding a script. When she reached her monologue she stopped, and then, instead of freezing, she turned to Laurie and said, "The line about the train station, is it 'she never arrived' or 'she was never arriving'?"

"It's 'she never arrived.'" Laurie said it, and Crystal nodded and said the speech straight through, both hands out flat like she was describing a table.

They ran it twice more before the custodian's keys sounded in the hallway. Tomorrow morning there would still be pages that were not memorised, and Laurie knew that what she had done tonight wasn't a solution so much as a bet, placed under duress, on an actor she had only four days of evidence to trust. It might not pay. But Crystal was gathering her things with the binder closed and tucked under her arm like something already behind her, and at the door she turned around. "Same time tomorrow morning?" she said. "Before everyone else gets here."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, a projectile's maximum height equals the square of its initial vertical velocity divided by twice g.
story:
The lab smelled like the rubber of stool feet and, faintly, of somebody's gum gone stale under the third bench, and Parker sat with a blank page of graph paper in front of him because that was easier than looking at the fence out the window, the one behind the soccer field that he had told Carlo he could clear with a baseball.

"Clear it," Carlo had said at lunch, "or buy the pizzas."

"Whole fence," Parker had said. "Over the top, not around."

Bastien had raised one eyebrow in a way that suggested he was holding a private plebiscite on Parker's sanity and that the vote was not going well. "It's like four meters. Maybe four and a half."

Parker had done what he always did with a claim he could not immediately support, which was to talk louder, and now, two hours later in the empty lab, the talking had worn off and left him with a page and the sinking, enervating feeling that he had wagered eight pizzas on nothing. He took out his phone and opened the slow-motion video Carlo had filmed of him throwing straight up against the brick wall, the throw where he'd given it everything, and he counted frames. Nine meters per second, roughly, straight up. He wrote it down.

Mr. Desir came through with a stack of quizzes and a mug that said WORLD'S ADEQUATE PHYSICIST, and he paused at Parker's page long enough to read it upside down. "You know the vertical and horizontal don't talk to each other," he said. "Up is up. Sideways is sideways." Then he went into the supply closet, which was how Mr. Desir delivered most of his wisdom, in passing, and let you decide whether it had been wisdom at all.

Parker stared at the nine. Carlo would say the throw was about the fence, distance, arc, all of it tangled together, one heroic athletic gesture. Bastien, who was quietly the most perspicacious person either of them knew, would say to take it apart. So Parker took it apart. If he threw at an angle, only part of his speed went up; the rest went sideways, carrying the ball toward the fence but doing nothing for height. Whatever angle he chose, the vertical part was the only part that mattered for clearing the top. He drew two arrows off one dot, one up, one across, and then the sentence from Tuesday's notes surfaced, in his own handwriting, which he trusted less than other people's: maximum height equals the initial vertical velocity squared divided by twice g.

He squared nine. Eighty-one. Twice g, with g at 9.8, was 19.6. He worked the division twice and got the same answer both times, about 4.1 meters. If he threw everything straight up, nine meters a second of pure vertical velocity, the ball would top out at four point one. The fence was four and a half.

Bastien arrived with a bag of chips and leaned over the page. "What's the number?"

"Four point one," Parker said. "If I throw at an angle it's worse, because the up part shrinks and the height goes as that squared." He tapped the arrow. "The across part just carries it, it doesn't lift it."

"So don't try it," Bastien said, and crunched a chip thoughtfully, the way other people stroked their chins.

Parker looked out the window again. Carlo was actually out there now, visible at the far edge of the field with two gloves and a ball, tossing it hand to hand and clearly conducting his own internal referendum, one that had pizza in the yes column and Parker's dignity in the no. There was something honest in the number that Parker found himself reluctant to give up. He had always thought of throws as single acts, will translated directly into arc, and it was strange and slightly wonderful to discover the whole thing came apart into two quiet strangers traveling at right angles, one rising and dying, one gliding on untouched. What stayed uncertain was whether knowing changed anything. A body could still outperform its filmed self; adrenaline was not in the equations. Or the fence could be four point two, not four and a half, because Bastien had paced it off in sneakers, and a pace is not a meter.

"You could still go out there," Bastien said. "Just to lose in person."

"Or," Parker said, capping his pen, "I could throw it straight up next to the fence and see how it looks next to the top."

Bastien considered this. "That's the most cowardly scientific experiment I've ever heard of."

They gathered the paper and the chips and went out through the double doors into the flat gold light of the field, where Carlo wound up and let one fly, high and long and nowhere near the fence, and Parker, holding his own ball, walked toward the top rail to stand beside it and see for himself.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: On the practical driving test in Great Britain, parallel parking at the side of the road is one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner may ask a candidate to do.
story:
Joseph had three weeks to learn what most people spread over a year, because in September he would be in Britain, at a university outside Leeds, and his mother had decided he should take his driving test there before term began. That left the practical matter of practice, and practice meant the car park behind Ferraro's Grocery, where Mr. Ramírez, who owned the store and the grey Corsa Joseph was borrowing, let him coned off a corner after closing. Tyce rode along most evenings, sitting in the back with his feet on the parcel shelf, calling out distances like a man commentating on golf.

"Left, down, slow, stop. That's a foot from the cone. Beautiful."

It was bay parking, mostly, because bays were what the car park had. Joseph got good at it. He learned the geometry of reversing between two painted lines until his hands did it without him, the way his hands found piano chords they'd forgotten. Merging he practised on the ring road at ten p.m., Tyce narrating from the back while the engine whined and Joseph's whole physiology seemed to funnel into his sweating palms, breath shallow, ears tuned to the pitch of the cars behind him. He learned to match speed in the slip lane, to look, signal, commit. What he had not learned, because there was no road with a kerb and parked cars to learn it on, was the parallel park.

He tried it anyway with the cones: pulling up alongside an imaginary car, reversing at an angle, straightening. He clipped a cone on Tuesday and knocked it ten feet, and Tyce retrieved it and said, "You'll want to expiate that one," and set it back in place with ceremony, as though restoring a grave marker.

On Thursday the worry arrived properly. Joseph had found a forum online where British learners traded their test stories, and he read them in bed until one in the morning, phone light on his face. Bay park, bay park, someone's test in Manchester, bay park in Leicester, and then a thread about someone who had only practised bays and drove home in tears after being asked to park at the side of the road between two cars. The examiners chose. You couldn't know which one you'd get. Joseph put the phone face-down and lay listening to the house tick, and then picked it up and messaged Avah, who had been in Sheffield since last year.

He woke to her reply, and read it twice at the kitchen table while his tea went cold.

"You're spiralling, so here's what I actually know. On the practical driving test in Great Britain, parallel parking at the side of the road is one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner may ask you to do. One of them. Bay parking is another. They pick, you don't. My flatmate got the bay and I got the parallel, same test centre, two weeks apart. So the answer isn't hope, it's do both. Is there a road near the store with cars parked along it? There always is. Go at a quiet hour. And stop reading forums, they're malevolent, I mean that literally, they want you frightened."

Tyce's shift at Ferraro's ended at six on Saturday, so that was when they went. Mr. Ramírez unlocked the lot gate for them and then walked home, but before he left he pointed up Church Lane, which ran along the side of the building, narrow, kerbed, with a dentist's office and a shuttered bakery whose customers left their cars nose-in to the pavement for hours. He said nothing about the test. He said only, "Nobody uses it on Sundays until the bakery opens at ten," and went.

At nine on Sunday the street was theirs, mostly. Joseph pulled up alongside a blue hatchback outside the bakery, checked his mirrors with exaggerated care, and reversed. He was slow, slower than the ring road had ever demanded of him, and the slowness itself was new information, the way precision lived at the bottom of the speedometer rather than the top. He came within a hand's width of the kerb and stopped crooked. Tyce got out, walked around, and stood looking at the gap between the tyre and the stone.

"Do it again."

They did it again, and again, moving up the street one car at a time, and on the fourth attempt Joseph left the car straight and close, and neither of them said anything for a second because both of them knew. Then a woman came out of the dentist's, unlocked a grey estate, and reversed out past them without hurrying or glaring, and Joseph watched her the whole time, the calm economy of it, the way she did in four seconds what had cost him ten minutes.

"Can I ask her something?" Joseph said, hand on the door.

"She's already gone, man."

But she hadn't. She had stopped at the end of the lane and was reversing into a space between two cars, smooth as pouring water, and Joseph put the car in gear and followed to watch, slow, at the side of the road.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A 'best before' date marks when a food's quality may start to decline, not when it becomes unsafe, so sealed food past that date may still be safe to eat.
story:
The food bank ran out of the library's basement, past the periodicals nobody read anymore and down a stairwell that smelled of damp paper and floor wax. Nolan had signed up because his mother said colleges liked to see it, which he suspected was true and which he resented anyway, since a good deed done for recompense of that kind seemed to him a shakier thing than no deed at all. He had not resolved the question by the time he reached the bottom of the stairs, where a woman in a cardigan the colour of weak tea was waiting for him.

"You must be Nolan. I'm Ms. Crowchild." She handed him a pair of blue nitrile gloves and a clipboard with columns for canned protein, canned vegetables, pasta, and miscellaneous. "Sort what's in the blue bins. Anything past its date goes in the discard barrel."

The blue bins held the leavings of a food drive at the high school: dented beans, off-brand soup, a single ceremonial tin of smoked oysters. Nolan worked beside a boy he knew slightly from chemistry, Hussain, who sorted fast and kept checking his phone against the clipboard like a lawyer billing hours. Hussain needed forty volunteer hours for a scholarship application, he said without being asked, and the deadline was Friday, and he did not have time for the miscellaneous column, which was where everything ambiguous went.

Nolan picked up a can of chickpeas and turned it over. The date on the bottom was eleven days past. He held it over the discard barrel and then didn't drop it, because the barrel was already half full and it had only been an hour, and it struck him as strange that a basement full of people who needed food should be generating this much waste. He looked at the can again. Best before, it said, not anything that sounded like poison.

"These say best before," he said to Hussain. "Not use by. Not expires."

"So?" Hussain said, not looking up.

"So maybe best before means something different." Nolan said it slowly, testing the idea the way you test ice. "Like, the date when the quality may start to decline. Not when it becomes unsafe. So if it's sealed, and it's only a couple weeks past, it might still be fine."

Hussain finally looked at him. "You sure?"

"No. That's the thing." But there was a rack of pamphlets by the stairwell, the kind nobody took, and among the ones about tenant law and winter boots was a single sheet about food dating from some provincial agency. Nolan read it twice. It said what he had guessed, in flat bureaucratic prose: a best before date marked when quality might begin to decline, not when food became unsafe, so sealed food past that date could still be safe to eat. He stood there holding the chickpeas and felt something shift that was less like being right than like being handed a responsibility he hadn't asked for, because now he had to decide what to do with it.

He brought the pamphlet to Ms. Crowchild. She read it, and her face did something complicated, irritation folding into something like relief. "We've been tossing them," she said. "The previous coordinator's rule. It was easier than arguing." She looked at the discard barrel, at the good sealed food sitting in it under a film of dust and crushed cracker boxes. "Easier isn't the same as right, though, is it."

They spent the next hour going through the barrel with hot cloths, wiping labels, pulling out the sealed cans that were only weeks or a few months past. Hussain helped, though he kept one eye on his phone and muttered that nobody had told him the scholarship committee gave credit for garbage archaeology. When they finished, the misc table held two full crates of recovered food, and Ms. Crowchild said the crates would go out with Thursday's hampers, and she put a photocopy of the pamphlet up on the wall beside the sorting instructions so nobody after them would make the same mistake. Nolan looked at the sheet of paper, its plain type, and understood that a small true thing, once posted, could outlast him here, and also that it was only paper and could be taken down by whoever came next. Institutions didn't ossify on their own. People let them, a can at a time.

Hussain left at four with his hours logged, shaking Nolan's hand with a formality that was half joke and half not. "If they call you for a reference," he said, "tell them I know my dates."

"I'll tell them you have metamorphic work habits," Nolan said. "You change under pressure."

"That's rocks, man."

"Rocks and you."

When the last bin was empty, Ms. Crowchild offered him the Thursday shift, handing out the hampers, seeing the food go to whoever it went to. He said he'd think about it, and meant it, because he still hadn't settled whether a good deed counted the same when you'd started it for an application, and because part of him suspected it didn't matter, that the chickpeas didn't care why he'd wiped them clean. He carried the discard barrel, lighter now, up the stairwell toward the late light coming through the library's front windows. At the top of the stairs he stopped, set the barrel down, and went back for one can of smoked oysters somebody had missed.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Sugar bloom is a dry, gritty white coating caused when moisture dissolves sugar on the chocolate's surface and the sugar recrystallizes as it dries.
story:
Maria had the bowl balanced on a folded towel before Anaya's kitchen door had fully closed behind them. "You can't just commandeer my double boiler," Anaya said, but she was already pulling the thermomètre her mother used for yogurt out of the drawer, so Maria counted that as permission. The chocolate was Anaya's, too, half a kilo of couverture bought online after they watched a video the previous Sunday, and the whole plan was Maria's: tempered chocolate by four o'clock, dipped strawberries, a snap you could hear across the room.

The method was more puzzle than recipe. Melt to forty-five degrees, cool to twenty-seven while stirring constantly, then bring it back up to thirty-one, warm enough to work but not so warm that the cocoa butter forgot its discipline. Anaya stirred the seed chocolate in while Maria read the temperature aloud, and between readings Maria kept glancing at the clock, because Cayden was coming over at three and she wanted the first batch done before he could eat the evidence.

Cayden arrived while the second batch was seeding, dropped his bag by the door, and stuck his head over the pot. "Why don't you just put it in the fridge?" he asked. "Everything sets in the fridge." Maria, who had privately thought exactly that at midnight on Wednesday, found herself defending the counter. "The cocoa butter forms the right crystals at thirty-one degrees," she said. "The fridge skips that." Cayden shrugged and stole a strawberry anyway, and Maria let it go, because she wasn't sure she could explain what she only half understood herself.

The first sheet set up beautifully. When Maria touched it, the surface was glass, and when she broke a corner off, it snapped so cleanly that Anaya yelped. They stood over the shards grinning like they'd discovered fire. "Okay," Cayden said, mouth full, "that's actually loud." Maria felt the peculiar satisfaction of a procedure obeying you because you obeyed it first.

The second sheet she did not have patience for. There were only three berries left, the pot was thickening, and Anaya's little brother was due home demanding the kitchen. So Maria slid the tray into the fridge, told herself it was just for speed, and went back to washing the bowls. Twenty minutes later she pulled it out into the humid warmth of the kitchen, and the chocolate looked wrong. Not melted, wrong. A dull, dry whiteness crept across the surface, powdery under her fingertip, gritty, like frost that had decided to become sand. She held the tray under the window light and turned it slowly, wondering how something so shiny could go so quiet.

"Condensation," Anaya said, leaning in, and Maria was already nodding, because she'd seen this once, in a photograph on a chocolate forum she'd scrolled past while pretending to study. The cold chocolate had sweated in the warm room, and the moisture had landed on the sugar sitting at the surface and dissolved it, and as it dried, the sugar came back as gritty little crystals, a pale crust where the shine had been. She looked it up to be sure and found the name almost immediately. "It's called sugar bloom," she read aloud. Cayden peered at her phone. "Bloom," he repeated, as if tasting the word. "Like flowers on a dead thing." Nobody laughed, exactly, but Anaya smiled into the dish towel.

Maria sat with the failed tray while the water ran, less annoyed than curious. The evening before, she'd have said the fridge was the clever shortcut, and Cayden had said it out loud for both of them. Now she turned the tray again and found she wanted to know which had ruined it, the cold or the warmth, the humidity or the hurry, and whether the same thing would happen to chocolate that had never been in the fridge at all, just left out on a muggy day. She could test that. She had Anaya's last bar and a whole August ahead.

"It's like historiography," Anaya said from the sink,scrubbing with more force than the pot required. "You can't understand why a war went wrong from one side's account. You need the temperature and the humidity and the fridge." Maria laughed, and then stopped, because it was almost true. She cut the bloomed chocolate into rough squares anyway, and Cayden ate one and pronounced it ugly but delicious, and she decided that a considered position could still end with your mouth full.

By the time the streetlights came on, the third batch sat on the counter in the warm kitchen, setting slowly, unsupervised, and Maria kept drifting past it with her phone's flashlight, checking for frost that wasn't coming, the way you check on something you don't entirely trust to be left alone. Anaya's brother had declared their whole enterprise moribund an hour ago, the strawberries long finished, and yet there Maria was, crouched at counter height, watching shine arrive one slow minute at a time. "You know we're going to do this again next weekend," Anaya said. Maria didn't answer. She was listening for the snap.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1966 experiment by Elliot Aronson and colleagues, a highly competent quiz contestant who spilled a cup of coffee was rated more likable afterward; this is called the pratfall effect.
story:
Eva arrived at the shop eleven minutes early, which she regretted immediately, because now she had nothing to do with her hands except fold and unfold the napkin in her pocket. The place had an ascetic look for an ice cream shop: white walls, two bare bulbs, a freezer case that hummed like it was holding a grudge. Linda was behind the counter, wearing the paper hat, stacking cones with the concentration of someone defusing them.

"He's real," Linda said, before Eva could ask. "Kathryn showed me his profile. He plays chess and quotes movies. So, manageable."

"He's late."

"He's four minutes late. Sit down before you enervate yourself standing there." Linda tapped the counter. "You want the usual? You'll order the usual. You always interrogate the menu and then order the usual."

Eva sat in the booth by the window. He came in at six minutes past, taller than his photos, and his hand knocked the water glass off the table before he had even finished saying his own name. The glass rolled, the water sheeted across the table and into his lap, and the napkin dispenser skidded to the floor and cracked open, scattering its insides.

"I'm so sorry." He was up, wiping at his jeans with the single surviving napkin. "God. Great. This is, this is already, this is a disaster. We should just, I can just go."

"You spilled water," Eva said.

"On myself. Before I sat down." He picked up the dispenser and tried to reassemble it, and the napkins kept sliding out. "You waited for a guy who spills things."

Eva pulled her psych notebook out of her bag, because it was in the front pocket and because it gave her something to do that wasn't laughing. There was a page from Mr. Augustin's class, the unit on impression formation, and the sentence she'd underlined twice. She thought about reading it aloud and decided against it, and then he sat down, damp and defeated, and she decided for it.

"There was an experiment in 1966," she said. "By Elliot Aronson and some colleagues. A quiz contestant who was highly competent spilled a cup of coffee, and people rated him more likable afterward. It's called the pratfall effect."

He stopped wringing out the napkin. "You made that up."

"Mr. Augustin made us memorize it. I got a B minus on that test, so." She slid the notebook across the wet table, and he read it, and something in his shoulders came down an inch.

"That's the most flattering thing anyone's ever said to me with a citation."

They ordered. Linda brought the sundaes and lingered just long enough to say, "He's clumsy, but he's read," and to leave before Eva could kick her under the counter. The conversation started and stalled and started again, the way first conversations do. He told her about his mother's restaurant, the summer it failed, how he still couldn't walk past the building. She told him about the college she was deferring from and the one she wasn't, and watched him decide not to offer her a bromide about how everything works out, watched him almost say it and swallow it, which she liked more than she would have liked the sentence itself.

But she caught herself, later, doing the arithmetic. The pratfall effect, the wet jeans, the way his failure had softened him in her eyes: how much of her liking him was him, and how much was the frame she'd set up before he even sat down? She had told herself she was being generous with the psychology, and maybe she was, or maybe she had just chosen her conclusion first and found the experiment to support it. She didn't know. The notebook was back in her bag and the question wasn't.

Outside, the streetlight came on and turned the window into a half-mirror, and she could see both of them in it, sitting across from a mostly empty dish.

"Okay," he said. "Your turn. Knock something over."

"You're joking."

"It's scientifically strategic. You said the competent ones get more likable. Prove you're competent first, then knock something over." He nudged the water glass an inch toward her with one finger.

Eva looked at the glass, then at the window, then at Linda, who was watching from the counter with the rag motionless in her hand. She picked up the glass, held it over the table, and waited.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In a car with anti-lock brakes, a driver in an emergency should press the brake firmly and hold it rather than pump it, and can still steer.
story:
Xavier's grandfather had driven him to the licensing office and insisted on coming inside, though the waiting room was already crowded and the plastic chairs were bolted in rows like something designed by a penurious city council. The old man had spent the whole drive lecturing. "When you have to stop fast," he'd said, gripping the dashboard at a red light as if it were a pulpit, "you pump the brakes. Tap, tap, tap. That's how you keep control. My father taught me that in a parking lot in 1968, and it saved my life twice."

"That's the car," the examiner at the desk said, pointing through the window at a white sedan with STUDENT DRIVER magnetic signs on both doors. A woman in her fifties was wiping the windshield with a rag, unhurried, thorough, the way a person cleans something they actually care about. Her lanyard said MS. MORETTI.

"Can I come along?" Xavier's grandfather asked.

"You can watch from the picnic table," Ms. Moretti said, not unkindly. She handed Xavier the keys. "It's his hour."

The picnic table sat under a scraggly maple at the edge of the lot, and Xavier's grandfather commandeered it like a general taking a hill, sitting where he could see the whole practice area, arms folded. Daisy from his chemistry class was there too, waiting for her own road test, and she waved at him through the glass with a grin he suspected he'd be hearing about on Monday.

The first forty minutes were unremarkable in the way good things are often unremarkable. He adjusted the mirror the wrong way, then the right way. He eased out of the lot without stalling, turned left on Ms. Moretti's quiet instruction, and discovered that the car responded to his hands the way a conversation responds to listening. "You're smooth," she said. "Most students grip the wheel like it owes them money."

Then, pulling out of the gas station on Mill Road, a shopping cart rolled off the curb island ahead of them, tumbling into their lane, and behind it a small dog, a terrier of no particular discipline, darting after it.

Xavier's foot went for the brake. His grandfather's voice arrived in his head, tap, tap, tap, and his leg actually began the motion, lifting, pressing, lifting, and the car lurched twice, still traveling, the cart still coming, and in the corner of his eye he saw the brake warning light flicker and something else, a pedal that pushed back under his foot, firm and strange.

"Press it," Ms. Moretti said. Not loudly. "Hold it down. Hard. And steer."

He pressed and held. The pedal buzzed under his shoe, and he steered, and the car stopped in a long straight shudder, six feet from the cart, and the terrier sat down in the middle of the lane as if it had accomplished something.

They sat in the ringing quiet. The dog's owner came running from behind the island, an old woman with a leash and no breath left, apologizing to the hood of the car.

"Anti-lock brakes," Ms. Moretti said, once the woman had towed the dog away. "You press firmly and hold it. You don't pump. And you can still steer while you're braking."

"That buzzing under my foot."

"That's the pedal," she said, and left it there.

Xavier looked at the picnic table. His grandfather had risen halfway out of his seat and was lowering himself back down, hand pressed flat to the maple's trunk, and Xavier understood that from that distance the lurching had looked like the beginning of a crash. He put the car in park, unbuckled, and got out, which was against some rule or other, and walked over.

"You okay, Grandpa?"

"Fine," his grandfather said, too quickly. Then, slower: "You were pumping."

"I know."

"Your great-grandfather," his grandfather started, and then stopped. He looked at the car, at the crumpled shopping cart being retrieved by a store employee, at Xavier's hands, which were still shaking a little. "That was a different kind of brake. Wasn't it."

"That's what she said," Xavier said. "I held it down and I could still steer. It stopped."

His grandfather nodded at the ground for a while.

They drove back with the windows cracked, and Daisy gave him a thumbs up through the glass as they passed, and Ms. Moretti wrote something on her clipboard and said he'd need more hours but that today counted. When he parked, his grandfather was standing at the curb, holding the folded rag Ms. Moretti had left on the picnic table.

"You dropped this," he said, to her.

She took it. "Thanks."

His grandfather opened the passenger door of his own truck and paused there, one hand on the roof. "So," he said. "When are you driving me somewhere?"

Xavier looked at his hands on the wheel, still in position ten and two. "Whenever you want," he said. "You can tell me about the old way the whole time."

His grandfather laughed, a sound Xavier hadn't heard in months, and got in the truck, and waited for him to pull out first.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: At a local maximum of a polynomial the derivative equals zero, because the tangent line at the top of the peak is horizontal.
story:
The library smelled like radiator dust and the cheap hot chocolate from the vending machine, and Parker had been at the corner table since fourth period, which meant his note sheet had gone from tidy columns to a grey smear of pencil. He was supposed to be learning derivatives for Monday's exam. Instead he was watching the door, because Arabella had texted him twice during lunch and then gone silent, which was not like her, and because she was the reason he needed the derivative in the first place.

She arrived at twenty past three with a laptop, a printed spreadsheet, and the expression of someone carrying a verdict. She sat down across from him, spun the laptop around, and showed him a graph. It was the sales curve for the senior fundraiser she was running, the one where profits climbed, peaked, and slid back down as they printed more shirts than anyone would buy. "The printer needs the final order by nine tonight," she said. "I keep guessing where the top is and I keep guessing wrong. Mr. Smith said you were the one in class who actually got the calculus unit."

"Mr. Smith proselytizes about calculus like it's a religion," Parker said, mostly to buy time, because in fact he had missed the day they covered exactly this, and the textbook chapter was open in front of him at a page he had read four times without it settling anywhere. Arabella, who had watched him talk his way through a chemistry lab with total confidence, believed him instantly, which was worse. She slid her notes closer and waited.

He started with what he knew. A polynomial, a function like her profit curve, had a derivative that gave the slope at every point. He could compute that much; the power rule was mechanical, almost soothing, and he filled half a page with it while Ben wandered over from the fiction shelves and leaned on the chair beside them, ostentatiously reading the spine of a novel he had no intention of opening. "You're frowning like an autocrat losing an election," Ben said. "Should I leave?"

"No, stay, he needs witnesses when this goes wrong," Arabella said, and Parker laughed, and then stopped laughing, because the problem was real and the deadline was real and she had trusted him in a way that made his stomach tighten. He had the derivative. It sat on the page, factored and tidy, and he had no idea what it was for.

He sketched her curve again, big this time, filling the margin of his notebook, and put his pencil at the left side where the profits climbed steeply. "Here the slope is steep," he said, dragging the pencil upward. "And here, near the top, it's getting less steep. And here, at the very top, it's flat for an instant before the curve tips over and goes down." He drew a short horizontal stroke with his fingertip across the peak. The three of them looked at it. "The tangent line at the top of the peak is horizontal," he said slowly, mostly to himself. "So the slope there is zero. Which means if I set the derivative equal to zero and solve it, I get exactly the x-value where the maximum is."

Arabella's head came up. "So the highest point is where the slope flattens out."

"That's it. That's the whole thing." He solved it right there, the numbers collapsing to a single value on both sides of the equation, and when he carried it back to her spreadsheet it landed almost on the nose, one row off from her best day of sales, which she said was close enough to make her petulant father's complaint about overprinting look exactly as wrong as she'd suspected. She pulled out her phone to text the printer a new number. Ben said, mildly, "So you didn't know that an hour ago."

"I didn't know that ten minutes ago," Parker said. He looked at his notebook, at the horizontal stroke he'd drawn across the peak, and at the derivative beside it, and he understood it in the way that mattered, not as a rule to recite but as something he had watched happen under his own pencil. Whether he could do it again Monday, cold, without a graph and two people watching, he honestly could not say. "Sit down," he told Ben, dragging the textbook across the table. "I need to do three more of these before I trust myself."

Ben sat. Arabella hovered over her phone, thumb paused above send, waiting for Parker to check her number one last time. He set the pencil at the base of the next curve and began to climb.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: All 50 US states and Washington, DC allow minors to consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission, though some states set a minimum age.
story:
The training was supposed to happen at the community center, but the community center flooded, so the eight peer health volunteers sat on folding chairs between the pharmacy's blood pressure machine and a rack of seasonal antihistamines. Ms. Greco, who ran the program, had given each of them a laminated card with three topics written on it: consent, contraception, and how to get tested. Jonathan read his card twice and put it in his back pocket.

"You're the educators now," Ms. Greco said. "Not preachers, not scaremongers. People will come in here with questions they're afraid to ask their parents. Your job is to have the answers ready." She tapped the counter. "Shadow the pharmacist till closing, then next Saturday you're on your own."

Shayden leaned over during the first slow hour. "This is pointless," he said. "Nobody's going to ask us anything. They'll ask the actual pharmacist."

"Then we'll know where to point them," Jonathan said.

"Besides," Shayden went on, lowering his voice, "it's not like anything happens the first time anyway. You can't get anything from one time. That's just science." The argument sounded complete to Shayden, but Jonathan had spent a semester learning to hear when a claim was specious, dressed up in the vocabulary of certainty, and this one had nothing under it. "That's not science," he said. "That's a thing people say so they don't have to think about it."

At six, Lili-Rose came in through the automatic doors with her jacket zipped to her chin even though it was warm out. She was in his econ class. She walked past them twice, then stopped at the condom display, picked up a box, read the back, and put it back, and stood there. Jonathan interpolated himself into her silence the way Ms. Greco had coached them, gently, with an offer rather than a question. "You can ask us anything," he said. "We're not store people. We can't tell anyone."

"I'm not asking for me," Lili-Rose said. Then, after a moment: "Okay, for me. Say somebody wanted to get tested. At a clinic. Wouldn't their mom have to sign something? Because I turned eighteen in March, but my brother's still sixteen, and I'm asking for both of us, kind of."

Jonathan didn't know. That was the honest position, and Ms. Greco had told them that honesty was the only thing they could never trade away. "I don't know," he said. "But I can find out while you're here." He had noticed, earlier, a carousel of pamphlets beside the pharmacy counter, the kind nobody read, and he went through it now: blood pressure, shingles, managing diabetes. Near the back, folded and slightly sun-faded, was one from the county health clinic about testing for infections.

He read it standing up, and then read it again sitting down, because the sentence was not what he expected. All fifty states and Washington, DC, it said, allow minors to consent to testing and treatment for these infections without a parent's permission, though some states set a minimum age. He checked the pamphlet's date, then the clinic's website on his phone, which said the same thing in plainer type. No mention of what their own state's minimum age was, no chart of the exceptions.
