The fact sat there without clearing up the part that actually mattered for her brother.

"Okay," he said, walking back. "So nobody has to sign for you. You're eighteen, but even for your brother, it's not a parent permission thing. Every state, all fifty plus DC, lets minors consent to testing and treatment without a parent. Some states have a minimum age, though, and I can't tell from this what ours is. So for you, nothing to worry about. For him, we'd have to call and ask one question."

Lili-Rose unzipped her jacket an inch. "It's not on any bill or anything?"

"I don't know that part," Jonathan said. "That's an insurance question. The pamphlet says the clinic has a sliding scale if you don't use insurance, but you'd have to ask them how it works." He watched her take this in. He could have smoothed it over, could have guessed, but the whole afternoon had been teaching him that a right answer delivered too fast was worth less than a slow one that was true.

"Would you walk over there?" she said. "It's four blocks. I know where it is, I just don't want to walk in alone."

The clinic was open until eight. Jonathan told Shayden he was leaving, took the pamphlet, and held the door. Outside, the light was going amber over the parking lot, and Lili-Rose walked fast, like someone with an appointment she'd already made in her head.

At the clinic's front desk, a nurse in lavender scrubs looked up from a keyboard. Lili-Rose opened her mouth, closed it, and Jonathan set the pamphlet on the counter between them. "She has a question about the minimum age," he said. "For her brother."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: The Keeling Curve zigzags every year because Northern Hemisphere plants take in carbon dioxide as they grow in spring and summer, then release it as leaves die and decay in autumn and winter.
story:
The assignment sheet said each of them had to staff an exhibit for two hours on Saturday, and Clara had drawn the climate wall, which meant she had to explain greenhouse gases to strangers without sounding like she was reciting a textbook. She had practiced in the mirror the night before, and the result had been discouraging, a string of phrases she half understood herself. On the bus to the museum she went through it again, mouthing the words, and an old woman across the aisle smiled at her as though she were praying.

The climate wall occupied a corner of the second floor, between a diaphanous curtain that shifted with the air from the vents and a case of carbon crystals labeled graphite and diamond. Ms. Ramos was waiting there with clipboards, allotting each student a badge and a laminated sheet of talking points. "You're not there to lecture," Ms. Ramos said. "You're there to answer questions. If you don't know, say so." Clara clipped on the badge, which read VOLUNTEER SCIENCE GUIDE, and felt like a fraud in a costume.

Mason had the shift beside hers, at a touch screen where visitors could scroll through a century of carbon dioxide measurements taken on a mountain in Hawaii. The line climbed steadily, but it wasn't smooth; it sawtoothed, rising and falling and rising again, dozens of small zigzags stacked along the upward slope. When a man in a running jacket squinted at it and asked what all the little wiggles meant, Mason said, "Oh, those are probably measurement error. The instruments back then weren't very good." The man nodded and moved on, and something about the ease of it bothered Clara, the way a wrong answer can allay curiosity better than a hard one.

She went over after her first visitor left. "Did you just make that up?" she asked.

"I inferred it," Mason said. "Sensors glitch. It's logical."

"But they're regular. Look." She dragged the screen back ten years, then forward again. The zigzags repeated on a schedule, peaks and dips arriving like tides. "Glitches don't keep a calendar."

Mason crossed his arms. "Fine. Then what are they?"

She didn't have an answer, and the not having it sat in her like a stone. She thought of her mother, who last spring had read a headline about record heat and said, "They can't even measure the temperature right, remember that scandal," and Clara had let it go because arguing at dinner cost more than she wanted to pay. She had chosen peace over precision, and she still wasn't sure it had been wrong, but she was sure she didn't want to do it again with a graph in front of her.

A school group came through, younger kids, one of whom pressed her palm flat against the exhibit's infrared panel so she could feel her own heat reflected back. Clara found herself explaining it more simply than she had in the mirror: some gases in the air let sunlight through but hold onto the heat that comes back off the ground, so the planet warms like a parked car with the windows up. A girl asked whether that meant the gases were bad, and Clara said no, that without them the nights would freeze, that the problem was how much, not that they existed. The girl considered this with what looked like actual fairness, and Clara felt the stone shift a little.

When the group moved on, she came back to the screen and stood in front of it, tracing one year's rise and fall with her finger. Up, then down, then up higher than before. She thought about the diamond in the case behind her, how the same carbon could be one thing or another depending on arrangement, and how the same graph could be noise or signal depending on what you knew. Then it landed, all at once, the way an answer sometimes does, and she grabbed Mason's sleeve.

"What happens to trees in spring?" she said.

"They grow. Leaves come out."

"And every fall?"

"They drop them. They die and rot." He stopped. His eyes went to the screen.

"That's your wiggle," Clara said. "Plants take in carbon dioxide when they grow in spring and summer, and when the leaves die in autumn and winter, it goes back into the air. The whole Northern Hemisphere breathing once a year. It's not an error, it's the forest."

Mason was quiet for a moment. "I told that guy in the running jacket it was the instruments."

"So go find him."

"He's gone. Probably thinks we're idiots now."

"Then find the next one." She pointed across the hall, where the man in the running jacket had circled back and was standing at the crystal case, reading about carbon with his hands in his pockets.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that 10.0 percent of wage and salary workers were union members in 2025, down from 20.1 percent in 1983.
story:
Vanessa found her grandfather in the break room of the warehouse, sitting on a folding chair with his lunch pail open and untouched. She had come to interview him for a sociology assignment, and he had waved her past the loading dock where he still worked two mornings a week, past the pallets shrink-wrapped in plastic that caught the light from the high windows like ice. He was seventy-one. He had worked here, or in buildings like it, since before she was born.

"Ask me anything," he said, "but let's walk. My knees lock up."

They walked the long aisle between the shelving, and Vanessa held her phone flat like a clipboard, recording. She asked her first question, the one she had rehearsed: had his working life been what he expected?

He laughed, a short sound that surprised a forklift driver into looking over. "Nobody expects a warehouse," he said. "You end up here and then you find out what you can make of it." He told her about 1983, when he started, when nearly everyone he worked beside carried a union card. "Half the country, more or less," he said. "Twenty point one percent of wage and salary workers. That was just normal." He said it the way he'd recite a batting average.

Vanessa stopped walking. "Twenty percent?" She thought of the numbers she had found that week, squinting at them in the library until they resolved. "It's ten now. I read that ten point zero percent of wage and salary workers were union members this year, 2025. Down from twenty point one in 1983." She had assumed she'd misread it, that there was a decimal in the wrong place, that some intervening paragraph would restore the world to its usual shape.

"You read right," her grandfather said. "I could count on one hand the people here who pay dues now."

They came out at the far end of the aisle, where a corkboard hung by the time clock, layered so thick with notices that the cork had become merely the substrate for other people's announcements, a lost earring, a car for sale, a shift swap. Near the bottom, half-covered, was an old contract schedule, the wage grid from a bargaining agreement three decades old. Her grandfather peeled back a corner of the notice above it without removing it. "Thirty-five years I watched that grid climb," he said. "Every three years we sat down across a table and argued, and the arguing was the point. Overtime after eight hours. Safety glasses paid for. Somebody couldn't just decide you were part-time on a Tuesday."

Kalli's voice came down the aisle before Kalli did. She was finishing her own shift, hair tied up, and she fell into step with them easily, the way she did everything. Vanessa had told her about the assignment, and Kalli had been skeptical in the way of someone who had worked nonunion since she was sixteen. "My manager just gives us what she can," Kalli said. "When she can. Last month it was a raise, this month it's fewer hours."

"That's the difference," Vanessa's grandfather said, but he said it gently, and he didn't elaborate. He had a way of leaving a sentence open like a door.

They stood by the time clock while workers punched out, one after another, each check of the machine like a small full stop. Vanessa watched a woman she didn't know pause to copy her hours from the board into her phone, careful, deliberate, the way her own mother kept receipts. She thought of her grandfather's phrase, sitting down across a table, and of Kalli's manager deciding alone, and she tried to verbalize what she was beginning to see: that the first arrangement distributed power and the second depended on goodwill, and goodwill was weather.

"I want to say unions are just better," she said to Kalli, "but I don't actually know yet what it costs. Dues. Rules. My grandfather got laid off in the nineties and the union couldn't stop it."

"The union got you severance, though," her grandfather said.

"See, that's the part I can't get straight," Vanessa said. "What it fixes and what it only slows down."

They walked out through the receiving door into the late afternoon. The lot was half empty, the cars of the morning shift already gone. Kalli said she had to run and asked, over her shoulder, whether Vanessa would share the interview audio, because there was a nascent effort among some of the evening crew to at least ask about predictable schedules, nothing formal, just a question put to management together rather than one at a time. "Like a first step," Kalli said. "Before anybody decides anything."

Vanessa said she would send it that night. Her grandfather drove her home with the windows cracked, and neither of them turned on the radio. In her room she opened her laptop, titled the document, and wrote the first line: "In 1983, twenty point one percent of wage and salary workers belonged to unions; in 2025, it was ten point zero percent." She sat looking at the sentence for a long moment. Then she pressed record on her grandfather's interview and listened to him say, again, "You end up here and then you find out what you can make of it."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: If people trust a central bank to keep inflation low, they ask for smaller wage and price increases, and that expectation itself helps keep inflation down.
story:
The automatic doors were still warm from the afternoon when Charlie clocked in, and aisle three smelled like crushed cardboard and floor wax. She had taken the job in June for the discount and the paycheck, but by August she had begun to notice that the shelves themselves were a kind of text. She would collate the shelf tags in her mind at night, the way Mr. Bouchard, her economics teacher, had once told them economists collate price data, and she had watched the pasta tag go from 1.19 to 1.39 to 1.49 without any of the boxes getting heavier.

That was what she was supposed to explain in her college interview on Saturday: how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. She had the first half down cold. Higher rates made borrowing expensive, so people bought fewer houses and cars, and with less spending, sellers stopped raising prices. What she could not fit into the explanation was the second half, the part Mr. Bouchard had circled on her practice essay with a question mark beside it, and her reflection in the freezer case every night carried a low hum of foreboding when she thought about it.

Elody was already at the register when Charlie came through the break room. Elody had a way of looking up before you spoke, as if she kept half an ear pointed at the door for whoever needed her next. "You look like you're studying with your face again," she said. "Interview stuff?"

"Saturday," Charlie said. She told her about the question mark, about the half of the explanation she couldn't find.

Elody rang up a carton of eggs for a woman with a tired toddler and didn't answer until the receipt was in the woman's hand. Then she said, "My mom asked for a raise last month. Three dollars an hour more. She said everything's going up anyway, so she'd better get hers first."

Charlie restocked cans of beans into the pyramid the day manager liked and found she had stopped hearing the scanner beeps. She was thinking about Paulina, who ran the lemonade stand at the farmers market on Saturdays. Two weekends ago Paulina and another girl had stood behind the pitcher arguing in the heat about raising the price from a dollar to a dollar fifty. "Everything's going to cost more next month," Paulina had said. "Cups, sugar, lemons. If we don't raise it now we'll lose money later." The other girl had said people would just stop buying, and they'd lose money anyway, and the two of them had looked at Charlie, standing there with her grocery bag, waiting for her to pick a side.

She had said, that day, that it depended on whether the lemonade would really cost more next month, and both girls had groaned at her. But now, sliding the last can into place, she saw what Mr. Bouchard's question mark had been pointing at. Paulina wasn't raising the price because lemons were expensive today. She was raising it because she expected them to be expensive tomorrow, and she wanted to get ahead of it. The expectation itself was doing the raising, before anything had actually changed.

Then the rest arrived all at once, the way the answer to a crossword clue does when you stop staring at it. If Paulina had believed the lemons would stay cheap, she would have kept the price at a dollar. She would have asked for less. It worked for wages too, like Elody's mom asking for three dollars more because she expected everything to climb. People who trusted the prices to stay put asked for smaller raises and smaller price increases. And a central bank that people trusted to keep inflation low did part of its work just by being trusted, because that trust made everyone ask for less, and the asking for less itself held prices down. It was strange, like a promise that kept itself. She still wasn't sure she could say where the trust came from, or what happened when it broke, and she supposed a real interviewer would want to know that too.

At nine, when the store emptied, she found a marker in the office and wrote on the back of a receipt roll: rates make borrowing costly, that's the visible half. The invisible half is what people expect. She looked at it, then added: but I don't know how trust is built or repaired, and I'm going to say that on Saturday. The sentence made her feel lighter and worse at once, like carrying groceries upstairs in one trip.

She came back out to find Paulina waiting by the registers with an empty glass jar and a receipt for string and sugar, standing in the fluorescent light like she owned the store's whole night. "Cups went up again," Paulina said. "I'm charging a dollar seventy-five on Saturday."

"Come to the interview with me," Charlie said, and watched her friend blink. "You're my second half. You're the part I couldn't write."

"Charlie, it's a lemonade stand."

"Exactly," Charlie said, and started counting out Paulina's change.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: In his 1865 book The Coal Question, William Stanley Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines made coal cheaper to use and increased Britain's total coal consumption.
story:
The hose at the community garden had split again, and Eli knelt in the mulch trying to tape it while Raine held the spigot half shut so the spray wouldn't soak them both. The water came out turbid at first, brown with whatever had sat in the pipes overnight, then cleared. They were watering Mr. Lau's plot because Mr. Lau was at the pharmacy until six, and because Eli owed him for the tomatoes he had crushed with the wheelbarrow in June.

The problem Eli actually wanted to solve had followed him from school. The town had spent a year replacing every streetlight and school fixture with efficient bulbs, and Keiran had gotten hold of the utility numbers through his internship at town hall. Total electricity use had gone up, not down, and people at the council meeting had used the word "scam." Keiran printed the spreadsheet and brought it to the garden, and now it sat on the upturned bucket between the bean rows, weighted with a rock against the breeze.

"It doesn't make sense," Keiran said. "Same number of lights. Less power per light. How does the bill go up?"

Raine let the spigot run while she pulled a weed from between the squash. "Maybe people just left them on longer," she said. "My dad does that now. Says it doesn't cost anything."

Eli had been quiet through most of the watering, and not only because of the tape. He'd read something in the spring, in a used economics book he'd bought for two dollars from the library cart, and the spreadsheet had reminded him of it. He didn't say it yet. He turned the paper so Keiran could see the column where the town's totals were charted month by month, a line climbing gently upward through a year of efficient lighting.

Mr. Lau arrived early, carrying a paper bag of plums, and sat on the bench by the fence to wait for them to finish. When Keiran complained loudly enough, Mr. Lau asked what the trouble was, and Eli told him about the bulbs and the rising bill.

"There was an economist," Eli said. "William Stanley Jevons. In 1865 he wrote a book, The Coal Question. He noticed that when steam engines got more efficient, coal got cheaper to use, and Britain ended up burning more coal in total, not less." He said it once, plainly, and then picked the rock back up off the spreadsheet because the wind had started again.

Keiran looked at the climbing line on the page, then at the garden gate, where the new lamp on the pole burned even in the daylight of early evening. "So cheap light means more light."

Raine wrung out the wet rag and hung it on the fence. "Then the town shouldn't vilify the bulbs," she said. "The bulbs work. It's us. We light things we never used to light because now it's easy." She pointed down the path, where a strip of decorative lamps along the flowerbeds glowed pale orange against the dusk, installed the same season as the retrofit, nobody having argued that they were necessary.

Eeli thought about his own house, where his mother sent a remittance every month to his grandmother and had been pleased, that first autumn, to discover the smaller line on the electricity bill. She had used the difference to run the dryer more often instead of hanging clothes on the line. He had not thought of it as anything until now. He didn't think the town was wrong to buy the bulbs, and he didn't think his mother was wrong to want the dryer. He thought both things were true at once, and that the town's mistake, if it had made one, was promising that efficiency alone would lower consumption, as if the number could be made to behave by machinery alone.

"Keiran," he said, "you're presenting to the council on Thursday, right?" Keiran nodded; the internship required it. "Don't tell them the bulbs failed. Tell them the bulbs worked and something else grew to fill the space. Then tell them about the lamps by the flowerbeds. Let them decide whether they want them."

Keiran folded the spreadsheet along its old creases. Mr. Lau split a plum with his thumbnail and offered half to whoever wanted it, and Raine took it. The water in the repaired hose ran steady now, and Eli held the nozzle over the tomato stakes while the last of the light went out of the sky overhead and the new lamp at the gate clicked on, brighter than the old one had ever been.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act, non-exempt employees must be paid one and a half times their regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek.
story:
Caleb folded the application across the table three times before handing it over, as though the creases might make it harder for the manager to reject. The restaurant, a family place called the Riverbend with vinyl booths and a laminated menu, needed a dishwasher and a weekend busser, and Caleb needed money for textbooks in the fall. The manager, a broad man named Mr. Adebayo who owned the building and lived above it, read the form in silence for a long moment. "You can start Thursday," he said finally. "School comes first, though. If your grades slip, you're done." Caleb said he understood, and he mostly did, though the word sinecure, which his father had used about some cousin's office job, floated through his head and made the whole thing feel suddenly real. This was not that. This was a sink and a hose and eight dollars an hour.

The first two weeks were scrapes and burns and the smell of onions in his hair. Then came spring break, and Georgia, who worked the register and had been there a year, asked him a dangerous question. "I need next weekend off," she said, wiping down the counter while the lunch rush drained away. "My sister's recital is in Columbus and I never get to see her dance. If you take my Saturday and Sunday, I'll owe you." Caleb looked at the schedule taped to the kitchen door. He was already down for Monday through Friday over break, full days, because two other staff were away. Adding Georgia's weekend would push him past forty hours, though he didn't think of it that way at the time. He thought only of the number at the bottom of his next check.

Mr. Adebayo agreed to the swap with a warning. "Payroll closes Sunday night," he said. "Get your hours to me by then or they roll to the next check." That became Caleb's deadline, and he kept a notebook in his back pocket, transcribing each shift into it at the end of every night: date, start, finish, initials from whoever closed the till. He was careful in a way that surprised him, careful the way he was careful with his college essays, as if the notebook were an argument he might someday have to defend.

The Thursday of break, Hadley texted him from the alley behind the restaurant, where the staff smoked even though none of them were old enough. "did u see ur hours," the message said. "check the stub from last week. u went over 40." Caleb was at home, sitting on his bedroom floor with the pay stub and his notebook spread out, and he counted. Monday to Sunday he had worked forty-six hours. The stub listed two rates. Forty hours at eight. Then six hours at twelve, one and a half times his regular rate, because under the law anything beyond forty hours in a workweek had to be paid that way. He read the stub four times. He had not known. Nobody had told him, and it had simply appeared, like a door in a wall he'd assumed was solid.

He texted Georgia first, wanting to share the discovery, and her reply arrived while he was still holding the stub. "thats how i paid for my prom dress last year. worked 52 hours one week. mr a says its the law, he won't fight it, but he watches the schedule like a hawk so nobody stacks extra on purpose." Then she added, "also please still take my weekend. i'll transcribe ur friday shift into the book myself if u want, i know his handwriting drives u crazy." Caleb laughed at that, alone on the floor, and then stopped laughing because a thought arrived that felt almost malevolent in its precision: if he took Georgia's shifts, his total for the new week would climb past fifty hours, and Mr. Adebayo, who had been kind to him, would have to pay a rate he clearly tried to avoid owing.

On Saturday, Caleb came in early and found Mr. Adebayo at the back booth doing invoices. "I can take Georgia's shifts," Caleb said, "but I know what it costs you. What if I take Saturday only, and you give Sunday to Hadley? He wants the hours, he told me." Mr. Adebayo set down his pen. He studied Caleb the way he studied the schedule, looking for the trick. "You are negotiating with me over six dollars an hour you haven't earned yet," he said. It was not a question. "Yes," Caleb said, and then, because honesty seemed safer than strategy, "I don't know if I'm doing it for you or for me. If I take both days I make more. If I split them, Hadley gets a bigger check and Georgia still gets her recital." Mr. Adebayo was quiet long enough that Caleb could hear the dishwasher thudding through the wall.

"Split them," Mr. Adebayo said at last, and wrote it on the schedule in his terrible handwriting. Then he looked up. "Sunday night, eleven o'clock, the book closes. Get your hours in." Georgia came through the kitchen door with her jacket already on, bound for Columbus and the recital, and she stopped when she saw the schedule. She read it, then read it again. "You gave Sunday to Hadley," she said. "I'll pay you back for this somehow." Caleb pulled out his notebook and began copying down his Friday hours, the numbers small and exact under the date. "Start with Saturday," he said. "I'll take it in onion rings."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Concussion guidelines say an athlete with a suspected concussion should not return to play on the same day, even if they feel fine.
story:
The heat on the baseball diamond rose in visible sheets by the third inning, and Elliot stood at shortstop watching the dust of the base paths delimit the field's whole world, a small square of chalk and dirt inside which, for one more summer, everything mattered. Dhruv was on the mound. Martina kept score behind the backstop, her pencil ticking like a metronome. The season had two weeks left, and Elliot wanted the championship game more than he had wanted anything he could name, which was why, when the collision happened, he was already running before his mind caught up.

The throw home pulled the catcher, Sam, a sophomore nobody counted on much, into the baseline, and the runner came through him shoulder-first. Sam went down in the chalk, the ball loose in the dirt, and the run scored, and for a moment nobody moved at all. Then Sam sat up, shook his head, and said the worst possible thing. "I'm fine. Put me back in."

The coach was already jogging out, and Elliot heard himself say, "You can't." The words came from somewhere specific. In the spring he had taken the online concussion module for a hockey clinic, half-asleep at his laptop, and one line had stuck because the instructor repeated it like an epigram, short and final: an athlete with a suspected concussion should not return to play on the same day, even if they feel fine. He had assumed it was about hockey. Standing on the dirt now, watching Sam blink against the sun, he understood it had never been about any one sport.

Sam got belligerent in the way only a kid who has been invisible all season can. "I'm not hurt. I caught two innings already, I know how I feel." His voice cracked on the last word, which argued better against him than anything Elliot could say. Martina had come to the fence, and Dhruv walked in from the mound, ball in his glove, sweat cutting pale lines through the dust on his face.

"He was out of it for like five seconds," Martina said quietly. "I saw it from the fence. He was somewhere else."

The coach crouched in front of Sam and asked him questions Elliot couldn't hear, and Elliot stood there hating every part of his own certainty. He thought of his father, who had played four years of college ball and told stories about getting his bell rung and going back out the same half-inning, stories told with pride, and Elliot had always received them as instruction. Two ideas sat side by side in him and did not merge: the guideline he had spoken aloud, and the older code that said you finish what you start, that sitting out was a kind of lie about yourself. He did not know yet which one he actually believed, only which one he had acted on.

Sam stood, took off the mask, and did not argue again, which was somehow worse than arguing. He walked to the fence with the slow, careful steps of someone testing a floor, and Elliot put on the spare catcher's mask, its sweat-smelling padding cold against his cheeks, and squatted behind the plate for the first time in two years. His knees remembered the position before his head did. Dhruv struck out the next batter on three pitches, and Martina's pencil ticked, and the game went on the way games do, indifferent, and they lost by one run in the bottom of the seventh when a ball Elliot should have ranged for landed in short left.

Afterward, in the shade of the dugout, Sam sat at the far end with an ice pack he wasn't holding against anything. Elliot carried the water cooler past him, stopped, and said, "I wasn't trying to take the game from you." Sam looked up, and his eyes were clear, and he said, "I know. That's what makes it weird." He didn't say more than that, and neither did Elliot. Martina closed her scorebook and put a hand briefly on Sam's shoulder, and Dhruv lay back on the bench with his cap over his face, and the sprinklers came on in the outfield, hissing, catching the low sun so that the whole grass went briefly gold.

Elliot took the mask off last of everything, and it hung from his hand by its strap as he walked out through the gate. There would be another game Saturday, and Sam would sit in the stands until the doctor cleared him, and Elliot still could not say for certain that the old code was wrong, only that he could no longer live inside it. A car horn sounded in the lot. He swung the mask up onto his shoulder and ran.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: The US fairness doctrine, introduced in 1949, required broadcasters to air contrasting views on controversial public issues; the Federal Communications Commission abolished it in 1987.
story:
The assignment sheet said "Compare two news reports on the same event," and Mr. Andersen had left the choosing to them, which Faith suspected was the whole point. She picked the mill closure on the east side of town, because her grandfather had worked there for thirty-one years and because the story had appeared everywhere, which meant she could hold two versions of it side by side like transparencies on a lightbox. One came from the site her phone defaulted to, which Hugo called "the one my dad yells at." The other came from the paper that had run a full-page ad for the company's redevelopment plan the same week.

"They're not lying," Nina said, leaning across the lab table to look at Faith's screen. "That's the annoying part. Everything in both of them is technically true."

"True in the way a portrait is true," Faith said, "if you only paint one side of the face."

Hugo, from the next table, contributed his opinion, which was that all media was garbage and you should just read the primary sources. He then asked Faith what a primary source for a mill closure would even be, and she said she didn't know, maybe standing outside the gate, and he said that sounded cold, and the conversation moved on, as conversations with Hugo tended to do.

At dinner that night her grandfather asked what she was studying, and when she said media studies he made a sound like a kettle deciding not to boil. "We used to have a rule about this," he said, spearing a potato. "The fairness doctrine. TV stations had to give both sides of a controversial issue, real time for the other view. Nineteen forty-nine, that started. The FCC, the commission that runs broadcasting, they abolished it in eighty-seven. I remember the stations complaining it was a burden." He said it the way he said most things about the past, as though reporting weather from a country that no longer existed. Faith looked it up after dinner, hunched over her phone at the kitchen counter while her mother washed dishes, and it checked out: 1949, the requirement to air contrasting views, gone in 1987. She sat with that for a while. It didn't tell her whether the doctrine had worked, or whether "both sides" was even the right frame, since some questions had three sides and some had none worth airing. It told her only that the information around her had a history, that the absence of a rule was itself a decision someone had made.

The next class, Mr. Andersen had them present. Nina led with the fact that the site owned by the company's former investor had described the closure as a "modernization," while the other had led with the workers, and Faith followed with the ownership question, tracing who held what, and it turned out to be less conspiracy than geometry: interests, angled, and light falling accordingly. She had planned to end on the fairness doctrine, a neat historical button, but standing there she found herself qualifying it before she could stop. "My grandpa remembers when it was the law," she said. "And part of me thinks that sounds fair, and part of me thinks fairness isn't the same as truth. You can give two sides equal time and both can be wrong." She paused, aware of Hugo watching her with the expression of someone whose easy cynicism was being made slightly less comfortable. "I don't know what the answer is. I just know the question didn't use to exist, and now it does."

Afterward Mr. Andersen asked whether she thought regulation was epistemology, whether a rule could actually change what a society knew, or only how it argued. Faith said she thought maybe arguing was a way of knowing, and he looked pleased in the way of a teacher who had asked a question without wanting a particular answer, which she found more unsettling than if he'd wanted one.

That night she went back to the two articles, and the affective weight of them struck her differently now, the way the adjectives moved her before the facts did, warm in one, cold in the other. Her grandfather called while she was reading, to ask if she wanted the rest of the plums, and she told him she'd used his rule in her presentation, and there was a silence on the line long enough that she thought the call had dropped.

"They abolished it before you were born," he said finally. "I keep forgetting that. You grew up in the after."

She looked at the two headlines, open in side-by-side windows, the same mill, the same week, almost unrecognizable as the same world. "I'm coming for the plums tomorrow," she said, and closed the laptop, and the screen held their ghosts a moment before going dark.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Freezer burn happens when air dries out the surface of frozen food; it makes food tough and tasteless but does not make it unsafe to eat.
story:
I was not nervous about leaving for college, which I told Sylvia three times on the walk to her house, once for each block. My mother had never taught me to cook because she preferred the kitchen to herself, and I had preferred being fed, so the arrangement had suited us both, and I said so with the confidence of someone who had never once considered what the arrangement would cost in September.

Sylvia's kitchen smelled like onions going soft in oil, and her mother had left a laminated sheet on the counter with seven dinners printed down the left margin. The logic of it seemed axiomatic to me immediately: cook on Sunday, eat all week, never stand in a grocery aisle at six in the evening with no plan and dwindling money. I said it was basically math. Sylvia said it was basically survival, and that her aunt had lost a whole term's grocery budget to takeaway before she figured this out.

We made a list together. Sylvia showed me how she planned around what would spoil first, spinach before carrots, and how she bought dried beans in bulk because cans cost four times more per serving. At the store I pushed the cart while she compared unit prices with a speed that mesmerized me, her finger moving down the shelf tags like a referee calling fouls. I bought my own copies of everything with the birthday money my grandmother had sent, forty dollars, which I told myself would stretch further than it did.

Back at her house we cooked in batches, chili and a stew and a tray of roasted vegetables, and we portioned them into containers. Sylvia pressed the lids down and slid a knife through the middle of the stew in each one. "Flat freezes faster," she said, "and air is the enemy." I wrote that in my phone under a note titled COLLEGE, and I believed I had learned it, the way you believe you've learned to swim from watching someone swim.

The trouble came two weeks later, after I had actually moved in. My first Sunday cook went well enough, or I recorded it that way in messages to Sylvia, telling her the stew had been perfect and my roommate was jealous. This was not entirely true. The stew had been thin and I had salted it twice, but the narrative I was building needed a success in it, so I supplied one. What I could not narrate around was the white, dry patch on the surface of the third container when I pulled it from the shared freezer on a Thursday, hungry and late from a lecture.

I stood at the microwave holding the container like evidence. The patch was grayish white and looked the way frost looks on the October fields back home, or the way I imagined the dry season looked on a savanna, cracked and pale across the top of something that had been living. I texted Sylvia a photo. Throwing out food I had paid for with my grandmother's money seemed unbearable; eating it seemed possibly dangerous.

She called instead of texting back. "That's freezer burn," she said. "Air dried out the surface." I asked if it would make me sick, and she said no, it was safe, it just turned the food tough and tasteless. Safe but ruined, or ruined but safe; I turned the container over in my hand, thinking that this was somehow the most useful thing anyone had told me all month, a small clean fact with two edges.

I ate it, because hungry is hungry, and she was right about tasteless, though I would later describe the meal to Sylvia as "fine, honestly fine," and she would reply with a single emoji of a raised eyebrow. The next Sunday I pressed plastic wrap down onto the surface of each portion before snapping the lids on, and I labeled the containers with dates, and I moved my cooking day earlier so the food would cool completely before it froze, all of it a considered assembly of what my mother never taught me and what Sylvia did and what the freezer itself had made plain.

I still didn't know whether the stew had actually been better that second week or whether I only wanted it to be, and I decided I could live inside that uncertainty the same way I was living inside everything else, three hours from home with a note in my phone called COLLEGE that I opened and added to while the water boiled. At the bottom, under a heading that just said next, I typed: tell Sylvia about the first stew. Then I typed: maybe. The water started to roar behind me.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Test-driven development, popularized by Kent Beck, follows a 'red, green, refactor' cycle: write a failing test, make it pass, then clean up the code.
story:
The whiteboard at the front of room 2C still said CODING CLUB in dried-out marker from September, and Ms. Desir had never bothered to wipe it. Isla set her laptop on the long table beside Kael's and opened her half-finished project before her bag even hit the floor. For three weeks she had been building a program to catalog her grandmother's succulents, the ones she'd inherited in July along with a handwritten list of Latin names, and she wanted it done before the club's showcase on Friday.

"Show me," Kael said, sliding his chair over. He was the only other person who had committed to presenting, and he'd been smug about his progress all month.

She turned the screen toward him. She had a class called Plant with fields for species, pot size, and watering interval, every field marked private, and getter methods lined up beneath them like little soldiers. She scrolled to the bottom, where a single lonely test checked that a Plant could tell you its species.

"That's it? One test?"

"It works," Isla said, though she heard how thin it sounded. She ran the test. A green bar appeared. The bar transfixed her for a moment, the way a green bar always did, proof of something finished, and then she noticed Kael was grinning.

"Raine did her whole project backwards," he said. "You want to see backwards? Raine, show her."

Across the table, Raine spun her laptop around. She had no class at all, as far as Isla could see. Just a folder of test files and a lot of red.

"What is this," Isla said. It wasn't a question so much as an accusation.

"It's test-driven development," Raine said. "Kent Beck popularized it. You follow a red, green, refactor cycle. Write a failing test, make it pass, then clean up the code." She tapped her screen. "I'm at red. I'm very good at red."

"That's truculent," Isla said. "You're being truculent about failing on purpose."

"Deliberately failing is a skill," Raine said, "and yes, I will be putting that on my college applications."

Isla looked back at her own green bar and felt, for the first time, that it was mocking her. She had written the class first, then one test to decorate it, and the test had passed the first time, which meant it had told her nothing. She'd been so pleased with the tidy phylogeny of her code, Plant at the root and Succulent branching off beneath it, that she'd never asked whether any of it actually behaved. Her watering interval field was an int. What happened if she set it to zero, or to negative three? She didn't know. She'd never checked.

"Okay," she said. She closed her project without saving a comment she'd been drafting and opened a new test file instead. She typed a test for a negative watering interval before writing a single line of the class that would handle it. She ran it. Red. The compiler complained that the method didn't exist, which was the point, which she was starting to understand was the whole point. She went back, added the smallest piece of code that could make the test pass, ran it again, and watched it go green. Then she deleted a getter she'd written two weeks ago and never used, because Raine leaned over and asked what it was for and Isla couldn't answer.

They went around like that until the hallway lights clicked to half. Ms. Desir drifted past on her way to the photocopier and paused long enough to say, "Red, green, what's the third one?" and Isla said "refactor" without looking up, and Ms. Desir said "huh" in a way that suggested she'd expected a different club entirely.

By six o'clock Isla had eleven tests and a class half the size it had been that morning. Three of the tests were still red, sitting in a row like stalled traffic, and she could not tell yet whether that meant her design was wrong or her expectations were. She packed her charger slowly, watching the screen dim.

"Showcase's Friday," Kael said at the door. "You're going to stand up there and show them a broken program?"

Isla zipped her bag. "I'm going to stand up there," she said, "and show them exactly which parts I don't know yet."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In the UK, students apply to university through UCAS and can choose up to five courses, listed in no order of preference.
story:
Austin had told everyone at school that he had already submitted his application, which was true in the sense that he had created an account, chosen a password, and then spent four evenings staring at the course search like a man trying to read a menu in a language he almost knew. The form sat open now on the family computer, cursor blinking in the box where the choices went, patient as a debt collector. His mother called it "the British thing." His father called it "the expensive thing." Austin called it UCAS, because that was the word at the top of the page, and he was beginning to suspect it was also the name of some ancient spirit that fed on the indecision of eighteen-year-olds.

The problem, as far as Austin could reconstruct it, was that he had eleven courses and some smaller number of slots. He had assumed, in the way he assumed most things, that the slots would be ranked. You put your dream school first and your safety last, like a wedding toast that starts with flattery and ends with an anecdote. So he was genuinely surprised, on Thursday night, when Emy-Rose leaned across the desk in the library and pointed at his screen.

"They're not in order," she said. "You get five courses, and they're listed in no order of preference. None. The universities can't tell which one you love best."

"Then how do they know whether to feel flattered?"

"They don't. Nobody imputes anything to anybody. It's just a list."

Austin sat with that. It struck him as either a brilliant act of mercy or a small conspiracy against people who enjoyed ranking things, and he was, regrettably, one of those people. He kept a tiered list of the coffee shops near school. He had once ranked his cousins. It wasn't that he thought order was truth; it was that order felt like armor, and UCAS had apparently confiscated it at the door.

Manraj, consulted at lunch, was no help, or was help in the way a fire is help in the cold. "Just pick the five best ones," he said, mouth full of chips.

"Best by what measure? Admission odds? Course content? Distance from a decent train station?"

"You're overthinking a form that doesn't even want your ranking. That's like alphabetizing your prayers."

"Prayers," Austin said, "are absolutely in order of desperation."

Manraj laughed so hard the chips were nearly lost, and Austin wrote nothing down, but he kept turning the no-order thing over on the walk home. If the list carried no preference, then what it carried was something else. Possibility, maybe. Five doors that all opened the same amount. The system seemed to be saying: we know you are eighteen; we know you do not actually know what you want; stop pretending you do. He found this either very wise or very alarming, and he genuinely could not decide which, which he suspected was the point.

Mr. Reyes, who lived two doors down and had apparently been to university in Britain at some point in the Jurassic period, was watering his roses when Austin passed with his backpack. Austin, who was not in the habit of talking to neighbors, surprised himself by stopping. "Is it true the list doesn't have an order?" he asked. "Five courses, no preference, nothing?"

"Five and no order," Mr. Reyes said, and squinted at his roses as though checking whether they agreed. "I spent a week deciding which to put first, and then a week realizing it hadn't mattered. Best two weeks of my life, in some ways." He did not elaborate, and Austin did not ask, because some doors you just knock on once.

That night, at the computer again, Austin did something he would later describe to Emy-Rose as strategic and to Manraj as a coin flip with extra steps. He made two columns. In one, the courses he chose for the version of himself who wanted to be practical: the sensible city programs, the ones with employment statistics. In the other, the courses chosen by the version who had, at fourteen, spent an entire summer reading about estuaries for no reason at all, a summer he had never mentioned to anyone because he could not explain the appeal without sounding unwell. He did not try to merge the columns into a ranking. He let them sit side by side, two perspectives on the same kid, and he noticed that three courses appeared in both columns anyway, which felt less like a coincidence than like evidence.

He was honest with himself about what remained unsettled: he did not know whether he was choosing out of genuine interest or out of a desire to seem interesting, whether the altruistic pull toward the environmental science courses was really about the planet or about being the sort of person who cared about the planet in front of other people. His nemesis, if he had one, was probably not the application form but the small voice that kept asking who was watching. He typed the five into the boxes, unordered, exactly as unordered as the system allowed, and hovered over the submit button.

"You're not ranked either," he told the list, and clicked.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: Raising interest rates tends to strengthen a country's currency by attracting foreign savings, which makes imports cheaper and puts downward pressure on prices.
story:
Aidan's grandfather kept a shortwave radio on the kitchen counter and a jar of pens that no longer wrote, and between the two, on Sunday afternoons, he kept the conversation going. Aidan had been coming to the house since September because his mother worked weekends and the house was closer to the library than their apartment. He sat at the table now with his phone open to the school trip page, where Ms. Castillo had posted the final payment schedule for the ten days in Madrid.

"Sixteen hundred," his grandfather said, reading over his shoulder without asking. "In my day that was a car."

"It's flights and the hostel and everything." Aidan scrolled to the spreadsheet Isabella had made, the one that broke the cost into euros and converted it, because Isabella believed in conversions the way some people believed in saints. "She keeps updating it. The euro number stays the same but the dollar one keeps dropping."

His grandfather turned down the radio and pulled out the chair opposite. "When did it start dropping?"

Aidan checked the history on the currency site. "Right after the central bank raised interest rates. Like a week after. Isabella noticed it first. She screenshotted everything." He turned the phone so his grandfather could see the chart, a line that had slid downhill for years and then, in one week, bent upward.

"Say it back to me, then," his grandfather said. He did this often, asked Aidan to say things back, and Aidan had learned that the old man was testing neither of them, only enjoying the shape of an argument. "Why would the rate move because of the bank?"

Aidan had read three articles on the bus over, and the pieces hadn't fit until Isabella had explained the trip budget angle at lunch on Thursday, and Benson had argued the opposite the same afternoon, loudly, with ketchup on his sleeve. "The bank raised rates, so savings here pay more. Foreign money comes in to get that interest. More money wants to be in dollars, so the dollar gets stronger. And when the dollar is stronger, imports get cheaper. Cheaper imports put downward pressure on prices generally. That's the whole chain." He said it and then heard it, the way you hear a sentence differently once it's out of your mouth, and it seemed both simpler and stranger than the articles had made it sound.

"And the trip?"

"The hostel bills in euros. If the dollar is stronger, my sixteen hundred buys more of it. Isabella recalculated and I owe about ninety less than the first version." He paused. "Benson says it doesn't work like that, that the bank just prints money and the rate thing is a coincidence. He got into it with Ms. Castillo on Friday. She wouldn't say who was right. She said to bring sources on Monday."

"Will you?"

"I have the chart. And the bank's own announcement." Aidan turned the phone off and then on again, a habit he had when he was deciding something. "Benson's my friend. I don't want to stand up in class and make it look like I'm correcting him."

His grandfather opened the jar of pens, took one out, looked at it as if surprised it still failed to write, and put it back. "There's a difference between correcting a man and correcting his arithmetic. The first one, nobody asked for. The second one, he'll thank you for in ten years or not at all." He turned the radio back up half a notch. "Though I'll grant you the timing is suspicious. You clearing the deck before you speak."

"That's not what it is." But it was partly what it was. Benson had lent him twenty dollars in October when his card had declined at the pharmacy, and had never mentioned it again, and Aidan had been carrying that twenty like a debt he couldn't expiate with money alone. He had looked up whether friendship obligated him to soften a fact, and had found no answer, and had then looked up whether a fact softened on purpose was still a fact, and had stopped looking.

"Make a judgment," his grandfather said. "Judicious doesn't mean timid. It means you've weighed it and you say the thing anyway."

On Monday Ms. Castillo called the trip meeting to order with the whiteboard still showing Friday's unfinished problem set. Benson came in late with his sources printed, three pages from a forum where someone called InflationHawk88 argued that central banks were theater. Isabella sat in the front row with her laptop open to the spreadsheet, and when Ms. Castillo asked for the rate question, Isabella raised her hand and said, "Aidan has the whole chain."

Benson turned around in his seat.

Aidan stood up with his phone in his hand, the chart projected huge and crooked on the screen, and walked through it the way he had at the kitchen table: the bank raises rates, savings here pay more, foreign money comes in, the currency strengthens, imports get cheaper, and cheaper imports put downward pressure on prices. He pointed to the week the line bent. "I'm not sure how much of the drop in our trip cost is this and how much is luck," he said. "I can't separate those. But the direction is right, and Benson's forum post doesn't account for any of it."

"That's pedantry," Benson said, but he said it without heat, and after class he fell into step beside Aidan in the hallway and asked, almost quietly, "So how much do we actually owe now?"

"Ninety less," Aidan said. "Isabella has the spreadsheet."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: A naive narrator, such as Huck in Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, reports events honestly but misunderstands them, so readers see more than the narrator does.
story:
The book club met in the back room of Mr. Grewal's shop on the first Thursday of the month, between the shelf of remaindered biographies and a radiator that clanked like something trying to escape. Victoria arrived early, as she always did, and set her copy of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn on the table with the sticky notes bristling from it like feathers. She had read it twice. She had a thesis. She was sixteen, and she intended to be right.

"I think he's lying to us," she said, before anyone had settled. "The whole voice is a performance. Nobody talks like that on the page by accident."

Arianne pulled off one glove finger by finger, the way she did when she wanted time to think. "He's not lying. He's a kid telling it exactly like it happened. That's the whole point. He reports everything straight."

"Then why is it funny?" Matis asked. He had brought his little sister's highlighted copy by mistake, and the pink streaks had spread through it like a rash, endemic to every chapter, so that no page survived untouched. "The bit with the wreck, and the snake, and him praying for the wig. If Huck's telling it straight, who's making the joke?"

Victoria opened her mouth to forestall whatever soft compromise was coming, because she could feel one coming, the way you feel rain. "Twain is," she said. "Twain stands behind him laughing."

"Then the narrator's unreliable," said the retired teacher at the end of the table, the one everyone called Mrs. Chair because she always claimed it. "Case closed."

Arianne frowned at her book. "He's not unreliable. He's the most reliable person on that river. He never once tells us something that didn't happen."

The argument went around the table twice and got nowhere. Victoria left with her sticky notes intact and her thesis wobbling, and that was the part she hated most: not losing, but not knowing whether she had lost.

That night Matis sent her a photo of one highlighted page with the caption: read the part where Huck says he'll go to hell. i read it 4 times. i don't think he gets what he's saying. victoria typed and deleted three replies before finding one she could stand by. she wrote: he means every word of it and still misses the meaning. it's like he's honest and wrong at the same time. matis replied: that's a weird combo. is there a word for it? she stared at the screen, because there was a word, she was almost sure, something she'd skimmed past in the appendix of the edition at the library. she wrote back: give me till thursday.

She went at lunch on Wednesday, alone, past the noisy cafeteria where a kind of performative ennui had settled over the ninth graders slumped around the vending machines. In the library's quiet she found a handbook of literary terms and ran her finger down the pages. There it was. She copied it onto her arm in pen because her notebook was in her locker, and she walked back through the halls with the ink showing at her cuff.

The scene through Arianne's eyes, later, would look like this: Victoria arriving at the shop on Thursday with her sleeve pushed up, sitting down before the radiator had finished its first complaint, and saying, "I was wrong. Partly wrong. Arianne, you were right, and I was right, and it's both, and it has a name. A naive narrator." She said the phrase carefully, the way you'd set down something breakable. "Huck reports events honestly but misunderstands them. He never lies to us about what happens. He lies to himself about what it means, without knowing he's doing it. So we see more than he does. That's why the funny parts are funny. He doesn't get the joke, and we do. We're standing behind him the whole time."

Matis put both hands flat on the table. "The steamboat wreck. He describes the whole con game falling apart and says it like it's weather. He doesn't get it and we're dying."

"Every scene works like that," Victoria said. "The praying. The slave hunters. You watch him do the right thing for the wrong reason and call it wicked, and your chest hurts, and he just keeps rowing."

Arianne was quiet for a moment, and Mrs. Chair, uncharacteristically, did not claim the last word. Mr. Grewal came through with a tray of chipped cups and set one within reach of everyone, nearest to Matis because Matis always forgot to take one. "So who do you trust," Arianne said finally, "when the person telling you the story can't be trusted to understand it?"

"That's the thing," Victoria said. "You trust him completely about the facts and you trust yourself about the meaning. Two different jobs. I don't know yet where the line is, exactly. I don't know how Twain keeps it from breaking." She turned to the marked page, the one Matis had photographed. "I only know it holds."

"Read it out," Matis said, and slid the book across the table toward her, pink and battered, already falling open to the right place.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Raising the temperature speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions, but it speeds up the endothermic direction more, which is why the equilibrium shifts that way.
story:
The chemistry exhibit on the third floor of the science museum was smaller than Christian had hoped, a single glass case with two sealed flasks, both holding the same reddish-brown gas. He leaned close to the placard. "Nitrogen dioxide at equilibrium," it read. "Watch what happens when we change the temperature." Inside the case, a small heater hummed beneath one flask while the other sat in a bath of crushed ice. Sadie stood beside him with her worksheet pressed against the glass, chewing the end of her pen.

"There," she said. "The warm one's getting darker. Write that down." She wanted the exhibit stamp more than she wanted the answer; there were six stamps scattered across the museum and a free pass to the planetarium for anyone who finished the sheet, and Sadie had been talking about the planetarium since the bus. Christian wrote something down, but he kept looking at the cold flask, where the brown was fading toward almost colorless, like tea diluted with milk.

He thought of the kitchen table in October, when his mother had shown him the two equations on his homework and said they were both happening at once, all the time, forward and reverse, and he had refused to believe it because it sounded like a machine running itself in both directions and staying somehow still. She had tapped the page. "Still isn't stopped," she said. "Still is balanced." He had pushed his chair back and gone to his room, and it had taken him weeks to stop feeling that the whole thing was a trick adults had agreed to believe.

Khalid arrived from the climate wing with a look of mild malaise, the kind he always got after reading too many wall panels about melting permafrost. "This one's better," Christian told him. "Look, they're heating it and it's getting more brown. That's backwards, isn't it? Heat should make everything faster."

Khalid squinted at the flasks. "So if it speeds everything up, the color should just stay the same but change faster. Like fast-forward." He glanced at Christian, and then at the worksheet in Sadie's hand, and then back at the flask, and the doubt on his face matched the doubt Christian felt in his own.

"But it doesn't stay the same," Sadie said, bored. "It went dark. Stamp, please, next room." Christian ignored her and walked to the other side of the case, where he could see both flasks at once. Both reactions were running both ways, forward and reverse, in both flasks. The heat hadn't stopped the reverse reaction, obviously. So what if heat sped up both directions, but not equally? He said it slowly, half to himself and half to Khalid. "Raising the temperature speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions. But it speeds up the endothermic direction more. That's why the equilibrium shifts that way." He looked at the warm flask, dark with brown, and then the cold one, nearly clear. One direction must be endothermic, and heat fed it harder than it fed the other, so the balance tipped, and the mixture stayed tipped as long as the temperature stayed high.

"Which direction is endothermic?" Khalid asked. Christian pointed at the cold flask, where the brown was disappearing. If cooling it pulled the color out, then making the brown was the direction that drank heat in. Khalid frowned at the flasks a long moment. "Okay," he said finally. "I change my mind. It's not fast-forward. It's like a seesaw with a kid who grows when it's hot out." Christian laughed, and even Sadie, who had been drifting toward the exit, drifted back to look.

Ms. Traoré, their neighbor from two doors down, who had insisted on driving them and was now pretending to read a panel about polymers, caught Christian's eye through the case. She raised an eyebrow, and he shrugged, meaning, I think I've got it, but maybe not all of it, because there was still something he couldn't pin down, some reason underneath the reason, and he wasn't going to pretend he'd reached it. The cold flask had gone almost fully colorless now. He put his hand flat on the glass beside it, close enough to feel the chill coming through, and watched the last trace of brown thin out toward nothing. Sadie tugged his sleeve. "Planetarium line's forming," she said. "Last one there sits in the back row."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: In the United States, a 100-year flood zone does not mean a flood every 100 years; it means the area has a 1 percent chance of flooding in any given year.
story:
The car smelled of gas-station coffee and the lawyer's office where Charlie's mother had spent the morning. They were four hours from home, in a city neither of them knew, because a house there was cheap in a way that made their realtor back home voluble with warnings and their landlord patient in a way Charlie distrusted. Her mother drove. Charlie rode with her laptop open on her knees, running the mapping software she'd been teaching herself since spring, the one Mr. Çelik, their neighbor, had shown her the first night over the fence, when he heard she wanted to study urban planning.

"Pull up the address again," her mother said, and Charlie typed it in. The parcel bloomed on the map, a small beige square with a porch in the listing photo, three bedrooms, a price that in their own city would not buy a bathroom. She had spent the week learning to layer things over these parcels: census tracts, median incomes, the ages of roofs. Now she dragged over a second layer, the flood map the Federal Emergency Management Agency published, and watched the colors change. The beige square sat inside a band of pale blue.

"What's that mean, the blue?" her mother asked, leaning toward the screen at a red light.

"It means the house is in what they call a hundred-year flood zone," Charlie said. The realtor, a man named only in Charlie's notes as Mr. Diaz, had said exactly that on the phone the day before, cheerful and certain: no worry, it's a hundred-year zone, you'd get a century out of it. Charlie had written it down because something about the sentence had snagged, the way a snaggle of syntax does, and she had looked it up that night in a motel room while her mother slept.

"Meaning a flood every hundred years," her mother said.

"No." Charlie heard her own voice come out flat, more certain than she felt. "It means the area has a one percent chance of flooding in any given year. That's all it means. That's the definition." She had read it twice, then a third time, because it rewrote the sentence the realtor had handed them. One percent a year did not add up to safety. Over the span of a mortgage it stacked, chance on chance, though she did not do that math out loud because she could not yet do it honestly in her head.

They met Mr. Diaz at the house itself, which stood trim and blond-bricked behind a row of young maples. He was warm, generous with the tour, full of detail about the schools. Charlie wandered the backyard with her laptop still under her arm, opened it on the picnic table, and overlaid the county's housing data on the flood layer. Then she walked the street on foot, the way Mr. Çelik had taught her, because a map was a claim and claims deserved a visit. The blue band followed the shallow creek two streets over, and the parcels inside it were not scattered. They were the newest and the cheapest houses, the ones built where the ground was forgiving to developers, and she could see the creek's flat tongue of land behind the fences.

Inside, she set the laptop on the kitchen island while her mother ran water in the sink. "You said it's safe for a hundred years," Charlie said. "It's a one percent chance in any given year. That's what the zone means."

Mr. Diaz looked at the ceiling, then at her mother, then at Charlie. "Honey, every house in this price range is in some zone." There was no menace in it, only fatigue, and Charlie understood something she had not expected to understand: he was not lying so much as rounding, the way everyone in the transaction rounded, the seller up, the appraiser down, the buyer toward hope. On the drive back that evening she told her mother this, and her mother was quiet for a long while, hands easy on the wheel, the city's lights coming on behind them.

"I still want it," her mother said finally. "Did you see that kitchen?" And Charlie, who had expected the map to end the argument, found instead that it had invigorated something harder: the choice itself, no longer a riddle with a right answer but a real thing with a price on one side and a probability on the other. She thought about arbitrage, a word from an economics video she'd watched at two in the morning, the trick of buying cheap in one market and dear in another, and thought that her mother was attempting it with their lives, trading a safe street they couldn't afford for a risky one they could. Whether that was wisdom or desperation was not something the software could compute. She closed the laptop and watched the dark fields go by.

"Let's sleep on it," her mother said, and signaled for the motel exit.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: An intersect overlay in GIS keeps only the areas that appear in both input layers, so intersecting housing with a flood zone shows just the homes inside the zone.
story:
The computer lab smelled like floor wax and someone's microwaved noodles, and Luca had been staring at the same map for eleven minutes. It was supposed to be his big idea for Ms. Ramírez's geography project: overlay the city's flood zones on the housing layer and find out which neighborhoods were actually at risk. The problem was that his screen currently showed every house in the city, all forty-two thousand of them, glowing like a rash of orange dots from the river to the interstate. "That's not a flood analysis," he said to nobody. "That's just a city with acne."

Lydiane slid into the chair beside him with her coffee that was legally soup, peered at his screen, and started laughing before she'd even set the cup down. "Luca. What did you do." She said it the way you'd ask a dog what it did to the couch. "Those are all the houses. You didn't overlay anything, you just stacked two maps and hoped."

"I didn't hope," Luca said, wounded. "I prognosticated." He'd found the word in his college prep vocabulary list that morning and had been waiting all day for a chance to deploy it. "I prognosticated that the software would know what I meant."

"The software is not your friend. The software does not love you." She spun his chair toward her, which was an unfair move, because now he couldn't even pretend to keep working. "Okay, look. You used the wrong tool. What you want is called an intersect."

Ms. Ramírez drifted past at that moment, hands in her cardigan pockets, and Luca froze like she might confiscate the whole conversation. But she only glanced at the screen, said "Mm," in the tone of a woman withholding judgment on purpose, and kept walking. Luca lowered his voice anyway. "A what."

"Intersect. It keeps only the areas that appear in both input layers." Lydiane grabbed a napkin and drew two sloppy circles, one labeled HOUSES and one labeled FLOOD, overlapping like a Venn diagram drawn by someone in a hurry. "So if you intersect housing with the flood zone, you get just the homes inside the zone. Only those. Everything else disappears." She tapped the overlap with her pen. "The houses you actually care about. Try it."

Luca turned back to the keyboard with the cautious optimism of a man re-entering a room where something has already exploded once. He found the tool, dragged the housing layer into the first box and the flood zone into the second, hovered over the button, and looked at Lydiane. She made a shooing gesture with her soup. He clicked.

The orange dots didn't vanish all at once; they thinned the way a crowd does when a movie lets out, draining away from the hills and the high ground near the mall until what remained clustered along the river in a long, patient smear. Luca leaned in until he could see his own reflection faintly in the monitor. Some of the dots were apartment buildings. Some were streets he recognized, the kind with porches and grill smoke in August. He zoomed until block names surfaced, and there was Miller Road, where his grandmother had lived until last spring, sitting four blocks inside the blue boundary of the flood zone like it had always known and never mentioned it.

"Whoa," said Mackenzie from two seats over, drawn in the way sharks and sixteen-year-olds are drawn to someone else's discovery. "Why is it all on one side of the river?" Luca scrolled, and it was true: the west bank was dense with surviving dots and the east bank nearly clean, which raised a question he couldn't answer from the map alone. Old zoning? The levee? Something about soil he hadn't learned yet? He wrote "WHY WEST?" on the back of his hand in pen, next to an old phone number he'd never called.

Ms. Ramírez appeared again, this time staying. She studied the screen with her arms folded, and Luca noticed she wasn't telling him anything, which he was beginning to understand was her entire method. "So this is the at-risk housing," he said, half to her and half to himself. "Just these. The intersect cut out everything outside the zone." He paused. "But I don't know why those houses are there. Or who lives in them, or whether the city already knows. The map tells me where, not why, not what anyone's doing about it."

"Good," Ms. Ramírez said. "That's the part worth finding out." She pointed at the cluster on the west bank. "Start with the water bill records at city hall. Public information." Then she smiled at his hand, where WHY WEST? was already smudging, and walked away humming something.

Lydiane raised her soup in a small toast. "Look at you. From city-wide acne to an actual question in one class period." Mackenzie, who was voluble in the way of people narrating everything they think, started speculating about levees and city council corruption and, inexplicably, his uncle's remittance payments to relatives overseas, all at once. Luca tuned him out and leaned back in the chair, which creaked like a small door. He pressed print. The printer on the far counter groaned, considered its options, and spat out the map, still warm, the orange dots scattered along the river like sparks someone hadn't swept up yet.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: French engineer Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone.
story:
Dominic hooked the harness strap under his arms and waited while Jon clipped the towing line to the weighted sled. The grass at the far end of the field was still wet from the morning's watering, and the sled's runners had cut two dark stripes into it on the earlier pulls. Behind him, the rest of the second string stood in a loose cluster, hands in pockets, watching the first string run sprints at the opposite goal.

"You're with Carly, Jon, and Dev," the coach said, checking his clipboard. "Four of you. Same load as last week. On my whistle."

They set their feet. The whistle went, and Dominic leaned into the harness, churning his legs through the first few metres. The sled moved, but slowly, slower than he had moved it alone two days before, when the coach had timed each of them one at a time and Dominic had pulled his best number of the season. Now, with three others on the same rope, the sled crawled, and Dominic could feel, through the line, a softness somewhere that was not his own. He stopped at the cone, gasping, and looked back. Carly was already unclipping, her face unreadable.

"That was ugly," Jon said, pulling his harness off over his head.

"It wasn't that bad," Carly said.

The coach said nothing. He wrote something on his clipboard, then called the next group. Dominic walked to the water station and stood there while the reverie of the single pull returned to him: the sled had felt lighter alone, or he had made it lighter, he could not tell which. He had wanted the number on the stopwatch more than anything that day. Today there was no stopwatch, only the coach's pen.

In chemistry, second period, Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya had them open their laptops for a research task, and Dominic typed the coach's words into the search bar instead: "group pulls rope less hard than alone." The first result was a scan of an old paper. A French engineer, Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, had found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone. Dominic read it twice. There was no mechanism in the summary, no reason, only the finding, and he sat with that for a moment, the same way he sat with a lab result that refused to match his hypothesis. He copied the name into his notes under a heading he did not show anyone.

At Thursday practice, the coach kept them on sleds. "Same groups," he said. "I want everything you have."

They pulled, and it was worse, or the same; Dominic could not distinguish. Afterward, sitting on the sled itself while the first string drank water, he told them. "There was this French engineer. Ringelmann. 1913. He measured it. People pulling a rope in a group each pull less hard than they do alone."

"So it's not us," Jon said.

"It's everyone. It's people."

Carly pulled a cleat out of the mud and looked at it. "So what do we do, pull alone forever?"
