Dominic had been turning that over since second period. Part of him wanted the finding to be a permission slip, a reason the sled had crawled that had nothing to do with anyone's character. Another part suspected that the finding described a tendency, not a law, and that a tendency was exactly the thing a group could decide to fight. He did not predicate his answer on either part winning. "I don't know," he said. "I think we could try counting. Out loud. Same rhythm."

"That's stupid," Jon said, but he stood up and clipped in anyway.

"On three," Dominic said. "One, two, three." They pulled on three, and pulled on every three after that, and the sled came off the wet grass faster than it had on Tuesday, not fast, but faster, and Dominic could hear Carly counting beside him, her voice a half-beat behind his, the two rhythms meeting and then holding together for the last ten metres. At the cone they collapsed, all four of them in a line in the mud, and the coach's pen moved across the clipboard.

"Better," the coach said. He did not say good.

Walking off the field, Carly caught up to him. "Was it the counting or did we just try harder today?"

Dominic thought about the question honestly, the way Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya kept asking them to. The counting might have done nothing; the number might be unchanged on some future Tuesday when they forgot. "I don't know," he said again. "Ringelmann didn't test the counting part."

"Typical engineer," Carly said, and swung her harness over her shoulder, and jogged toward the parking lot where the lights were just coming on over the empty goal.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: In most jurisdictions traffic already on a highway has the right of way, so a merging driver must adjust speed to fit a gap rather than expect others to make room.
story:
The cones were set up in the kitchen again, four of them marking a parking space between the island and the trash can, and Oliver eased the office chair between them with his hands at ten and two. "You're turning too early," Wilson said from the counter, where he was scoring Oliver's attempts on a sticky note. "You clipped the island. That's a curb. Automatic fail." Wilson had failed his own test twice, which made him, in his words, the world's leading authority on what not to do, a distinction he announced with genuine pride.

Oliver spun the chair back out and tried again. The whole thing had started as a joke, the chair, the cones, the sticky note scoreboard, but somewhere around Wednesday it had stopped being funny and become serious, the way games between them always did. His test was in nine days. The parallel parking was survivable; what scared him was the highway merge, and he had said so, out loud, once, to his mother, who had looked at him with such careful sympathy that he immediately wished he hadn't.

Skyler arrived with the good cookies and dropped into a chair to watch. "The chair doesn't have mirrors," she pointed out. "That's your whole problem. You can't merge without mirrors." She mimed checking one, exaggerated, and Wilson said she was being unhelpful, and she said she was being realistic, which in her vocabulary were the same word.

"I don't actually understand merging," Oliver admitted. He said it lightly, the way you confess to not knowing how to dance, but it cost him something to say. "I did the practice drive with my uncle. There was a transport truck in the right lane and I just, like, sat there. Waiting. My uncle had to grab the wheel."

Wilson laughed so hard he nearly fell off the counter. "Waiting for what? For the truck to get a nicer personality?"

"For it to move over. You know. To let me in."

Skyler stopped chewing her cookie. "Did it move?"

"It did not. My uncle said, 'Who yields here?' and I said the truck, obviously, it's bigger, and he laughed for the entire length of the on-ramp. Like, an uncomfortably long time. Then he told me and I felt like an idiot."

"In most places, traffic already on the highway has the right of way," Wilson said, in the tone of someone reciting a scar he'd earned. "The merging driver has to adjust speed to fit a gap. You don't get to expect people to make room." He held up his sticky note. "I learned this by stalling on a ramp in front of a school bus. The bus did not move over. Neither did anything else. There was honking. There was so much honking."

"So the truck was never going to move," Oliver said slowly. "It wasn't being mean. It just, it didn't have to." He looked at the four cones and the office chair, at his absurd kitchen highway, and tried to hold both ideas at once: that the other drivers weren't his enemies, and that no one was coming to save him either. It was oddly clarifying. The merge wasn't a negotiation or a standoff. It was his job. He had to find the gap and match it.

"Speed up or slow down," Skyler said, "but decide before the ramp runs out." She took another cookie with the calm of someone who had been driving for eight months and found the whole topic mildly enthralling in the way that other people's disasters always are.

"Okay." Oliver rolled the chair to the far end of the kitchen, where the tile met the hallway threshold, and said, "That's the ramp. Wilson, you're the truck." Wilson stood in the traffic lane, arms crossed, absolutely impervious to persuasion, having decided in advance that he would not move for anyone. "My kitchen, my rules," their friend announced from the doorway, where Oliver's mother had appeared with tea. "It's a theocracy up in here and I am the god of the slow lane."

Oliver accelerated along the tile, hunting for the gap between Wilson and the counter, and turned in clean, both cone islands untouched, and stopped with his hands still at ten and two. Nobody said anything for a second, and then Skyler reached over and moved the top sticky note to the side that said PASS.

"Eight more like that," Wilson said, "and the actual road has nothing to teach you." He reset the cones anyway.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A violin's four strings are tuned in perfect fifths to G, D, A and E, from lowest to highest.
story:
The violin case had a sticker on it that said PROPERTY OF NORTHGATE BAND PROGRAM, which Mia took as a personal insult, since she had been begging to borrow one for three weeks and only got it the day after Mr. Ramos returned from his sabbatical and found the request slip buried under a pile of them on his desk. She carried it into the band room before school, set it on a chair, and opened it like she expected something to leap out.

"You're holding it wrong already," said Tegan, who was tuning her flute with the smug patience of someone who had played since fourth grade. "The skinny end goes up."

"Thank you, I know which end is the skinny end." Mia lifted the instrument out and held it at her side like a lantern. The strings were a mystery to her. She had assumed, before she actually touched one, that the strings would be arranged in some obvious order, low to high, like a piano, like a staircase. They were not, as far as she could tell, arranged in any order at all.

She plucked one. It made a sound like a doorbell. She plucked the next one over and it made a lower sound, which confused her, because she had plucked the one to the right first and that one had been higher, and now she plucked the far left one and it was lower still, and none of it formed a pattern she could keep in her head.

"You're just going to have to memorize them," Tegan said, watching her in the stand lights like a nature documentary.

"That's what people who already know things say to people who don't."

Cameron came in with a bag of hash browns and sat on the timpani case, which was forbidden, which is why he did it. "Memorize what?"

"Her strings. She keeps grabbing the wrong one and it sounds like a dying goose."

"It does not sound like a dying goose." Mia plucked a string. It sounded like a dying goose. Cameron pointed at it with a hash brown, delighted.

Mr. Ramos crossed to the piano, keys still cold, and played a note, then another, then a third, letting each hang in the room. Then he walked over and plucked each of her open strings one at a time, in order from the lowest one up, without saying a word. Mia frowned. She watched his finger move left to right, lowest to highest, and something shifted in her head.

"Wait," she said. "Do it again." He did. G, D, A, E, from the lowest string up, and she heard it: each one was the same distance from the last, each one that same bright gap her mother's old records called perfect fifths, and they ran G, D, A, E in a straight climb. She said it out loud, "G, D, A, E, lowest to highest," and Tegan said, "There it is," and Cameron said, "Gee, Dee, Ay, Ee," in the voice of a man announcing a boat race.

"Good-dae," Mia said slowly. "It almost says something. Good-day. Good-day, E." She pointed at the highest string. "Good day to you, E, you tiny screaming one."

"Congratulations," said Tegan, "you have learned a greeting and a scale and it took you forty minutes."

Mia took the bow, which she had been avoiding because the bow felt like a thing that could hear her thoughts. She set it on the A string, the one in the middle of her good day, and pulled. The sound was thin and wobbly and alive, and it surprised her so much she did it again. Cameron clapped once, softly, like a golf audience.

She practiced the climb after that, G to D to A to E, over and over, until her left arm ached from holding the thing up and Tegan had packed her flute twice and unpacked it twice. Mia could feel the two ideas suturing themselves together in her mind, the order of the strings and the sound of the order, so that when she reached for a note her hand was starting to know where to go without her spelling it out first. It was not smooth yet. It was embryonic, as Mr. Ramos would probably say if he were being annoying about it, but it existed.

The bell rang for first period and everyone groaned and gathered their things. Mr. Ramos stopped her at the door, tapped the case, and said, "Tomorrow, the other direction. Highest to lowest." Mia stared at him, doing the climb backwards in her head, E, A, D, G, like a boat rowing home. "Good day," she told him, "in reverse." He laughed once, a real one, and Cameron, from down the hallway, shouted, "E says good day back."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and people who do not vote without a valid reason can be fined.
story:
Carson had the sample ballot folded into quarters in his jacket pocket, and by the third time he unfolded it at the corner table of the coffee shop, the creases had gone soft as cloth. Whitney watched him smooth it flat between two lattes and said nothing for a while, which for Whitney was a kind of courtesy. The election was in nine days. He would turn eighteen two days before it, which meant that for the first time in his life, the country was actually asking him something, and he could not decide whether that felt like being trusted or being handed a live wire.

"I keep going back and forth," he said. "My mom wants one thing, my uncle wants the opposite, and every time I read a news story it's like the story is writing the conclusion for me and just letting me watch."

"So don't read the news," Whitney said. "Read the boring stuff. The budget summaries. The things nobody argues about because arguing about them doesn't beguile anyone."

"That is the least helpful advice I've ever received, and yet." He turned his cup a quarter rotation on its saucer, a small wheel deciding nothing.

Ryley arrived then, shaking rain off a canvas bag, and dropped into the chair with the confidence of someone who has already formed an opinion. "I've decided I'm not voting," Ryley announced. "It's a symbolic refusal. The whole system is, like, sectarian anyway, two tribes yelling."

From where Mr. Adebayo sat with his crossword, two tables over, this carried clearly, as Ryley's pronouncements generally did. He looked up. He owned the shop, or at least managed it so thoroughly that ownership seemed a technicality, and he had opinions about everything, though he rationed them.

"A symbolic refusal," he repeated, as if tasting the phrase and finding it underseasoned. "In Australia, that would cost you money. They've had compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and if you don't vote without a valid reason, you can be fined."

Ryley blinked. "Fined? Like, actual money? For not showing up?"

"Actual money," Mr. Adebayo said, and went back to seven across, which was more than Carson could have managed, because something in Carson's head had just shifted gears without his permission. He sat with it, turning his cup again, and the thought that assembled itself was not elegant: everyone votes, so everyone is counted, so the tribes have to talk to people outside their tribes, or at least pretend to. It did not prove anything. He noticed it did not prove anything. But it was the first argument he had built himself, out of parts from two different shelves, and it held his weight when he leaned on it.

"You look like a man who has been given homework by accident," Whitney said.

"I think I just decided something," Carson said slowly. "Not who to vote for. Just that I'm going to, and that not going isn't a protest, it's just absence. Skipping a meeting doesn't make the meeting disagree with you." He looked at Ryley. "You can still refuse. But in Australia you'd pay for the privilege."

"This is why I don't come here," Ryley said, though Ryley came here four times a week. "Fine. Fined. Whatever. I'll think about it, which is more than I promised this morning."

Whitney, meanwhile, had gone quiet in a different register, and Carson watched the change happen without knowing its name. The truth was that Whitney had already voted, absentee, three weeks ago, the first of their circle to do it, and had told no one because the vote had gone the way Whitney's mother wanted and not the way Whitney's own reading of the budget summaries had wanted, and the vote was already sealed in an envelope in a mailbox in Ohio. There was no amnesty for that, no way to take it back, and the guilt was small but persistent, like a stone in a shoe that you keep meaning to shake out and never quite stop walking long enough to do it.

"Actually," Whitney said, "can I see that ballot again? The sample one." Carson passed it across, creases and all, and Whitney studied the local measures at the bottom, the school board line in particular, where a name sat that Whitney had not researched at all.

"Turns out there's more on there than the loud part," Whitney said. "Who's Kowalski?"

"No idea," Carson said. "That's what tomorrow's for, I guess."

Mr. Adebayo set down his pen. "Seven across," he said. "Eight letters, 'arrangement whereby no one can opt out.' It's not federation, I've checked."

"Compulsory," said three teenagers at once, and the man wrote it in.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Pomp and Circumstance became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905, where Edward Elgar received an honorary doctorate of music.
story:
Maxime had been asked to speak at graduation, and for three weeks he had not written a word. Now he stood at the edge of the gymnasium with his speech folded into his back pocket like a confession, watching the band run through the march for the fourth time that afternoon. The folded paper was actually blank. He had told his mother it was finished. He had told Mr. Rosen it was nearly finished. The ceremony was in two hours.

The chairs had been arranged in ranks across the basketball court, spartan rows without decoration, and the custodian was still taping down the extension cords. On the stage the band played the loop everyone knew, the one that climbs and climbs and never quite arrives anywhere. Maxime had heard it at his cousin's graduation, at an assembly in eighth grade, in a movie about a school he couldn't remember. It was the only music that meant this, and he could not have said why.

"Again from the top," said the band teacher, and Maxime drifted toward the folding tables where Kiersten was stacking programs. She was salutatorian and had written her speech in a single night, which Maxime found almost offensive.

"I'm going to pretend you have yours," she said, without looking up.

"I have the shape of it."

"You have two hours to find the shape of a shape." She squared the stack against the table edge. "Romy's asking whether you'll mention the thing."

There was a thing. Romy had proposed, in the parking lot on Tuesday, that someone should say out loud that the class had voted, narrowly, to keep the valedictorian speaking alone and cut the second speaker, and that the vote had not been about the speeches at all. It had been about a fight from October that nobody would name. Romy thought the truth was owed. Kiersten thought the truth, delivered from a stage, was just a slower weapon. Maxime had been caught between them for days, and the blank page in his pocket was partly that.

He wandered back toward the band, where a trumpet player named nothing to him, a sophomore he knew only as the kid who dropped mutes, was squinting at his music with an expression of private grievance. "Why is it always this song," the kid said, to no one. "Every school. Every year. Like it's a law."

Maxime, who wanted any excuse not to think about his speech, said, "Look it up."

"I don't get wifi in here."

"Then guess."

"Elgar wrote it, that's all I know. The guy who wrote it. So someone at the first graduation ever must have liked it."

The band teacher called the march again, and the loop began its climb, and Maxime, leaning against the bleachers, typed the question into his phone with his thumb. The gymnasium's dead air gave him one bar. The answer loaded slowly, sentence by sentence, and he read it twice. The march had become graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905, where Edward Elgar received an honorary doctorate of music. That was all. One ceremony, one honor given to a composer, and a century of gymnasiums afterward inherited it without asking.

He stood very still while the trumpet climbed again. It seemed suddenly strange to him that the most repeated ritual of his life had begun as an accident of one afternoon, an honor meant for one man. And yet the students in the chairs would cry at it anyway. They would cry precisely because it had been repeated until it meant this, the way a road worn by feet becomes the only way across a field. He thought of the vote, and Romy's demand for the truth, and Kiersten's warning, and understood that these were the same problem wearing different clothes: whether a thing is made true by how it began or by what people have agreed it means since.

He found Mr. Rosen by the doors, checking names against the seating chart. "I have a question about the speech," Maxime said. "If I only had one fact, and it was about how this music started, would that be enough?"

"Enough for what?"

"To stand between two people who both want me to say something worse."

Mr. Rosen looked at him for a long moment. "You're asking whether a fact can do the work of an argument."

"Maybe I'm asking whether it's fair to let it."

Then the hour was gone, and there was no more arbitrating to be done. The chairs filled. Romy, in line three rows back, caught his eye and raised an eyebrow, a question with a demand inside it. Kiersten, near the stage, did not look at him at all. The band lifted into the loop one final time, and Maxime walked up under the sound of it with his blank page in his pocket, unfolded it on the podium so it looked like something, and looked out at all of them.

"In 1905," he said, "they played this at Yale for one man." He watched the rows of faces, and the kid with the trumpet watching him from the stage, and Romy leaning forward, and Kiersten finally turning toward him at last. "And it became ours."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Each transfer RNA carries one amino acid and has a three-base anticodon that pairs with the matching codon on the messenger RNA.
story:
Logan had taped the butcher paper to the living room wall at eleven in the morning, and by noon it had begun to peel, which he took as a personal insult. The paper was divided into three long lanes. The first lane said DNA, the second said mRNA, the third said PROTEIN, all in marker so fat it had bled through onto the paint. His mother had looked at the smudge, looked at him, and gone into the kitchen without comment, which was worse than comment.

The exam was Monday. It was Saturday. Between those two facts lay the entire process of transcription and translation, which Logan could recite and could not, apparently, actually explain, a distinction Mr. Leung had made mercilessly clear on his last quiz. "You have written the words," his teacher had said, handing it back, "but the words have not written anything through you." Logan had spent two days deciding whether that was profound or just annoying.

Theresa arrived first, carrying a shoebox and a bag of chips she did not intend to share. Billy came twenty minutes later with the excuse that his bus had destabilized, which was not a thing buses did, and everyone let it stand because it was less embarrassing than the truth, which was that he had been playing a game in his basement and lost track of time.

"So we're the molecules," Theresa said, surveying the paper. She had opened the shoebox on the coffee table. Inside were maybe forty index cards, cut in half, which Logan had spent Friday night making instead of going to the thing he'd told people he was going to.

"You're the enzyme," Logan said. "I'm the DNA. Billy's the mRNA."

"Why do you get to be the DNA?"

"Because it's my wall."

Billy plucked a half-card from the box, read it, and held it up. It said, in Logan's handwriting, AUG. "What's this, a stock ticker?"

"It's a codon." Theresa said it with the flat patience of someone who had already done the reading. "Three bases on the messenger RNA. That's the whole point of you, Billy. You're the message. Logan gets copied into you, and then you get read."

Billy considered this. "So I'm a photocopy of Logan."

"A photocopy that gets eaten by a ribosome," Logan said. "Sit in the middle lane."

They worked it out physically, which was Logan's whole plan, the reason for the wall and the cards and the afternoon. He stood in the DNA lane and read his sequence aloud, base by base, and Theresa walked beside him in the mRNA lane writing each complement onto a fresh card, taping them into a long strip that snaked down the wall. When she finished, the strip spelled out a message in three-letter chunks, and Billy lay on the couch holding the end of it like a man holding a leash attached to nothing.

"Now the ribosome," Logan said. "That's the coffee table. Billy, drag your message over here. Read your first codon."

"AUG."

"Okay." Logan consulted the box. Each full card, the uncut ones, had a name written at the top, like Phe or Leu or Met, and three letters at the bottom. He found the one he wanted and handed it to Theresa. "You're the transfer RNA. This is yours."

Theresa read it out. "Met, and the bottom says UAC."

"And the top part is your amino acid," Logan said. "One card, one amino acid. That's all you carry. Just the one."

"And the three letters at the bottom?"

"The anticodon," Logan said. "It's called the anticodon. Three bases, and they pair with the matching codon on the messenger RNA. So when Billy says AUG, you say UAC, and they click together, and the amino acid gets handed over." He demonstrated, pressing Theresa's card against Billy's strip so the two triplets touched. "Then the ribosome scoots along, Billy reads the next codon, and a new tRNA shows up with its own amino acid and its own anticodon."

Theresa held her card against the AUG and made a small clicking noise with her tongue. "I have matched. I have delivered my single amino acid, my whole life's cargo. Now what?"

"Now you go get another card," Logan said, "and do it again, forever, until you die."

"Grim," said Billy, "for a molecule."

They ran the whole sequence that way, Billy reading codons off the wall in a game-show announcer's voice, Theresa ferrying cards from the box and clicking them into place, each one depositing its amino acid at the top of the third lane in a growing chain. Logan kept the pile of amino acids in order, taping them into a line: Met, then whatever came next, then whatever came after that, a meaningless word in a language of three-letter gibberish that was, he understood suddenly and with some vertigo, the language his own body was speaking in every cell at that moment, including the cells doing the understanding.

It fell apart at codon eleven. Billy read "GGG," and Logan, rifling the box, handed over a card without checking it, because Billy had made a joke about anticodons and Logan had been laughing. Theresa clicked the card into place. Two amino acids later she stopped, frowned at the chain, and walked back down the lane to codon eleven with the particular slow stride of someone who has decided to be right.

"This is wrong," she said. "The card says Leu, but the anticodon is CCC. That pairs with GGG, which is Gly. I'm carrying the wrong amino acid for my anticodon." She held the card up to the light as though that would help. "Logan. You mismade a card, or you grabbed the wrong one."

Logan checked the box. He had mismade the card, back on Friday night, probably during the hour he'd been half-watching a show with the sound off. He sat down on the ribosome, which is to say the coffee table, and looked at the chain of taped amino acids, eleven links of work, one of them wrong. He could argue that the card was a clerical error, not a conceptual one. He could argue that the process still worked, that the demonstration was sound. Both arguments were true, and neither changed the fact that the protein, if it had been real, if it had been a hemoglobin or an enzyme in an actual cell, would now be built wrong and would do wrong things, and there would be no one in the cell to notice.

"Theresa's right," he said finally. "We tear it back to eleven."

Billy groaned from the couch but peeled the tape. Theresa, reticent for a full minute, which for her was extraordinary, finally said, "You know, this is the first time it's made sense to me. Not the words. The actual matching. The anticodon finding its codon like a plug finding a socket." She re-taped the corrected card into place. "Wrong plug, wrong socket, wrong protein."

Mr. Leung, it turned out, was at the door, holding a plate of his wife's almond cookies, which he left with neighbors on Saturdays in a ritual no one had ever explained. He looked past Logan's shoulder at the wall: three lanes, a snaking mRNA, a half-built chain of amino acids, two teenagers on the floor surrounded by cards. He set the plate down on the arm of the couch.

"Monday," he said, to no one in particular, and left. Billy reached for a cookie. Theresa slapped his hand and pointed at codon twelve.

"Read," she said. "The ribosome is waiting."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The law of conservation of mass means the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants in a closed system.
story:
Grace told herself she had never been afraid of chemistry, which was easier than admitting she had spent the whole semester watching the board the way you watch a film in a language you half know. The proof she was fine, she said, was that she was here at the kitchen table at nine in the evening with the textbook open to the chapter she needed for Tuesday's placement retest, and fine people did that. Fine people also did not hide their first attempt at the exam in the drawer with the dead batteries, but she chose not to think about that part.

The problem on the page wanted moles of product from a given mass of reactant, and the book's method sat there in its four neat steps like a staircase she couldn't find the bottom of. Write the balanced equation. Convert grams to moles using molar mass. Use the ratio. Convert back. She understood each sentence alone. It was the space between them, the reason grams became moles became grams again, that kept sliding out from under her.

"You're doing that thing," her mother said from the doorway, towel over one shoulder, "where you read the same line twelve times."

"I'm absorbing it."

"You're glaring at it."

Her mother went upstairs and Grace turned the textbook sideways, as if the numbers might confess to something when caught off guard. Sixty grams of a reactant; find the moles of product. She had written 0.75 and crossed it out, then written 0.75 again, because prevaricate was apparently what her pencil did when her brain wouldn't. Somewhere in the drawer with the dead batteries was her first attempt, where she had divided by the wrong molar mass and gotten an answer that felt, at the time, satisfyingly precise.

What she kept circling back to was the science fair, eleventh grade, the spring before everything got hard to attend. Aleah had sealed baking soda and vinegar in a zip bag with a cheap digital scale taped to the table, and Grace had stood there for twenty minutes waiting for the number to change. It never did. "The bag's sealed," Aleah had said. "That's the whole trick. Law of conservation of mass." Arman had leaned in, unconvinced, tapping the scale until Mr. Grant, judging that aisle, told him to stop abusing the equipment. The number stayed put. Sixty-something grams before, sixty-something grams after, and Grace had walked away thinking it was a nice fact for other people to have.

Now she thought about it differently, and the thought arrived the way a smell arrives in a crepuscular room, before you can name it. If nothing escaped the bag, then every atom that went in had come out wearing new clothes. The gas and the water and whatever else were all still there, rearranged. So the moles she was calculating weren't a bookkeeping fiction; they were her way of counting the atoms that had to end up somewhere. The equation's ratio was a promise about where they went.

She got up and found the box of baking soda behind the coffee filters. Her mother's kitchen scale, the one with the temperamental battery contact, sat by the toaster. She weighed an empty bag, added a spoon of powder, sealed in a small cup of vinegar laid on its side, weighed it again, and wrote the number on her forearm with a pen because paper had betrayed her too many times tonight. Then, holding the bag over the sink like a person defusing something, she tipped the cup over.

The bag fizzed and tightened and went cold in her hand, a small exothermic no, a small something, and when the commotion settled she set it back on the scale. Same number. Down to the last gram the scale could see, the total mass of the products equalled the total mass of the reactants, sealed in, nothing lost. She stood very still, as if the atoms might notice her and rearrange back.

"Grace," her mother called down, "did something explode?"

"It worked," she called back, which wasn't an answer, and then, quieter, to the bag, "it worked."

She sat back down and did the textbook problem again. Sixty grams of reactant; she found its molar mass in the periodic table, divided, watched grams cancel and leave moles the way her arithmetic teacher used to promise they would, multiplied by the ratio from the balanced equation, and got a number that wasn't 0.75. She checked it twice. She still didn't fully understand why the ratio had to be read product-over-reactant rather than the other way, and she could feel that uncertainty sitting next to her like a polite guest, but the bag on the scale had told her something the textbook hadn't: the atoms were all accounted for, and her job was only to follow where they'd gone.

She texted Arman a photo of the bag with the scale's display in frame. He replied with a single question mark. She typed, "Remember Aleah's fair project? It's like that. Atoms don't leave, they just move," and then deleted it, because it sounded like something a person who had understood all along would say, and she was trying to stop telling that particular story about herself. She sent the photo alone instead, and started the next problem, pencil moving, the sealed bag still resting by the toaster, holding its quiet arithmetic.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In Edgar Allan Poe's 1843 story 'The Tell-Tale Heart', the narrator insists he is not mad while describing how he murdered an old man.
story:
Aaron had promised his mother he would be home by six, and the promise was already failing, because page thirty-seven of Edgar Allan Poe's 1843 story "The Tell-Tale Heart" had hooks in him that would not let go. He sat at the back table of the public library with the story open on one side and a battered biology textbook on the other, two subjects he had assumed were separate now refusing to stay that way. Mr. Buchanan had assigned the story on Friday with a single instruction: tell me who is speaking, and whether you believe him. At the time Aaron had thought the question was strange. The narrator was the narrator. Who else would be speaking?

"You're doing the Poe thing too?" Sloane dropped into the chair across from him and slid her copy across the table, its margins already crowded with her small, furious handwriting. "I've read it three times and I keep losing my grip on it. He kills this old man, and the whole time he's telling you he's not mad. That's what I don't get. If he's not mad, why does he keep insisting on it?"

Aaron looked down at the page, where the narrator was indeed protesting again, in that breathless, urgent voice, that what was wrong with him was an over-acuteness of the senses rather than any disease. He had a sudden memory of himself at thirteen, standing in the kitchen telling his mother he had not been fighting with Reilly behind the school, and how the more he insisted, the narrower her eyes became. He had been lying then. But the narrator in the story might not be lying, exactly. He might be telling the truth as he could see it, and the truth as he could see it was the problem. "Maybe that's the trick," Aaron said slowly. "The protests are what make us doubt him. A sane person wouldn't need to keep saying it."

Sloane leaned forward, tapping the table with two fingers. "So we can't trust him, but we can't get rid of him either, because he's the only voice we've got."

"That's the assignment, I think. Buchanan wants us to notice that the point of view is doing something to us." Aaron turned to the last page, where the narrator's composure came apart under the imagined beating of the dead man's heart. On the inside cover, someone had left a folded note, yellowed and soft at the creases, forgotten or abandoned. He almost set it aside, then opened it.

Dear whoever gets this seat after me, the note began. I have read this story eleven times over four years and I still don't know if the narrator is ill or evil or both, and Mr. Buchanan, who was irascible even then, gave me a C for saying so honestly instead of pretending to certainty. I have decided the C was fair. Certainty about another person's mind is always a kind of lie, even about a fictional person, especially about a fictional person. If you figure it out, leave a note of your own. I'll come back and look. It was signed only with the letter R.

"Reilly's, you think?" Sloane asked, reading over his arm. "He had Buchanan sophomore year."

"Reilly doesn't write like this." Aaron read it again. The handwriting was older, the loops more careful, the kind of hand that predated keyboards. He thought of Buchanan himself, the way he taught from the same battered paperback every year, the same coffee ring on the cover, the way he had paused for a long moment on Friday when he handed the story out, as though handing over something private. It occurred to Aaron, and the thought arrived fully formed and unwelcome, that the note might be Buchanan's own, written when he was a student in some other teacher's classroom, that he had assigned this story for twenty years partly to keep the question alive and partly to fish for the note he had lost. He had no evidence. He held the possibility lightly, the way you hold a suspicion about a friend.

His biology textbook lay open to the immune chapter, and his eyes drifted to it without permission. The body learns an antigen, the paragraph said, by responding to it, by building something shaped to the invader's exact contours; the response is the knowing. He thought that reading was like that too. The narrator's insistence was the antigen, and the doubt Sloane kept describing was Aaron's own response, built in the exact shape of the protests against them. He had been treating the narrator's voice as a wall between himself and the story, when it might instead be the thing his understanding was being made from. It was a small synthesis, and he did not yet know whether it would subsume Sloane's reading or merely sit beside it, uncomfortably, the way two true accounts of one afternoon can sit side by side.

He took out a pen. Sloane watched him write: I don't know either, but I don't think Buchanan wants us to. I think he wants the not-knowing kept in good repair. P.S. If this was you, sir, the coffee ring gave you away. He folded the note, pressed it back inside the cover, and shelved the book face-out on the return cart, where the next person would have to pick it up to see the title. Then he checked the clock, texted his mother that he was walking home now, really, and at the door he glanced back once. The cart was empty. Buchanan was standing at the far shelf with the paperback in his hand, not opening it, just holding it, and he did not look up.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: R. Edward Freeman's 1984 book Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach argued that businesses should consider everyone affected by their decisions, not only their owners.
story:
The motion for the semifinal was printed on the whiteboard in Mr. Ndlovu's looping hand: This house would require companies to weigh everyone affected by their decisions, not just their shareholders. Jasmine copied it into her notebook twice, once in ink and once in the margin in pencil, as though the second copy might mean something different.

"You're second speaker," Olivier said, dropping into the chair beside her. "I'll open, Norah closes, you do the heavy lifting." He had a way of making a compliment sound like a warning. The three of them had made it this far on a routine: Olivier charmed, Norah bulldozed, and Jasmine took notes until her hand ached, then stood up and dismantled the other team one card at a time.

The opposing school arrived in matching blazers, and Jasmine recognized their first speaker from a tournament in the spring, a boy who argued the way some people drive, fast and certain, checking no mirrors. He opened with efficiency. A factory owner owes his loyalty to shareholders, he said, because they carry the risk; spread responsibility too thin and it dissolves entirely. Everyone becomes answerable to everyone, which means no one is answerable to anyone. It sounded good. It even sounded wise, until Jasmine noticed it was specious, a smooth surface over a hollow center, because the workers who rode the bus for an hour to that factory carried risk too, only theirs came without dividends.

During the break she sat on the floor of the hallway with her notes spread around her like fallen leaves. Norah crouched beside her, chewing a pen cap. "You need a spine for this," Norah said. "One idea we can hang everything on."

"I might have one." Jasmine had found it at her part-time job the month before, when the manager reshuffled the schedule to keep the store open later, which helped sales and quietly stranded two closers who missed the last bus. She had gone looking for language to describe what she'd seen, that sickening sense that a decision could be correct and wrong at once, and in a library database she had found R. Edward Freeman's 1984 book, Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach. "He argued businesses should consider everyone affected by their decisions, not only their owners," she told Norah. "He called it the stakeholder approach."

"Say that in the room exactly like that," Norah said, and stood up.

When Jasmine rose to speak, the microphone hummed against her fingertips. She laid out the case for the workers, the bus riders, the town whose air the factory used like a free lung, and she gave them Freeman's name and year like a hand passed back through the crowd. But somewhere in her second minute she heard her own voice drift, and she stopped. Because the opposing boy was not entirely wrong either, and pretending otherwise was a kind of lying she had watched adults do all her life, letting their first position ossify into identity until no new fact could get through. "I want to concede something," she said, and the room shifted. "If a company answers to everyone, it can end up answering to no one. That's a real cost. I'm not sure the principle fixes it. I think it might just tell us what we're choosing between."

The judges' pencils did not move for a moment, then all moved at once.

They lost on points, two to one. The ballot said her concession had "weakened the closing," though Norah, reading over her shoulder in the corridor, snorted and said the judge simply preferred rectitude to honesty, a tidy column of right answers where none existed. Olivier bought three hot chocolates from the machine even though the button only worked if you hit it twice, and they drank them on the steps outside while the winning team's bus pulled away into the dark.

Jasmine turned her phone over in her pocket, thinking of Monday's shift, of the schedule taped by the time clock, of the two closers who would read it without complaint. Maybe she would ask the manager one question, plainly, and learn nothing she didn't already know. Maybe she would learn something. Norah nudged her shoulder and said, "Rematch next year. You keep the file?" Jasmine tapped her notebook, the pages still warm from the room, and said, "I'll add to it."
